chapters.title: Chapter 301: The Dao Language
paragraphs: Satisfied, Stan set the bottle back on the counter and turned his attention to the second item that had caught his eye.
[The Dao Language Primer]
It was a book. Another book, like the one he had purchased that afternoon, but this one bore a different title.
[Introduction to the Dao Language]

[A foundational primer for comprehending the script of Heaven and Earth, in which all true cultivation manuals are written. A required reference for any practitioner who wishes to read sect documents, ancient inscriptions, or the cultivation techniques offered within this shop.]
[Cost: 1 system point.]
Stan stared at the listing. A moment later, a missing piece clicked into place...
The cultivation manuals. The ancient sect records. The inscriptions carved into relics from the old world.

According to Introduction to Earth, they were all written in the Dao Language—the language of Heaven and Earth, a script lost to ordinary humanity because true comprehension required a level of Qi resonance that the modern world could no longer sustain.
Without it, the manuals in the shop were little more than beautifully bound books filled with indecipherable symbols.
The primer solved that problem.

The price was only one system point. He had deliberately converted more money than he had spent during his initial purchases, and a quick glance at his balance confirmed he still had a single point remaining.
He made the purchase without hesitation.
[Purchase confirmed.]
[Introduction to the Dao Language acquired.]
The book materialized in his hand.

It was noticeably slimmer than Introduction to Earth, a compact hardback bound in cream-colored cloth. The title was embossed across the cover in matte black lettering. There was no author’s name, no publisher’s mark, and no text on the back—only the title, presented with the quiet confidence of something that required no further introduction.
Stan carried it to the dining table, pulled out a chair, and sat down.
Then he opened it to the first Chapter.
INTRODUCTION TO THE DAO
’Ordinary languages were created by humans. The Dao Language was not.’
The opening line carried the same dry, almost academic gravitas as ’Introduction to Earth’.
Stan recognized the voice immediately. Whether it was the work of the same author or simply the same system, the writing possessed the same measured authority.

He read on. The Dao Language, the primer explained, predated humanity, civilization, perhaps even the world itself. The ancient cultivators who composed the great manuals had not, in any meaningful sense, invented a written language for their teachings. Instead, they had recorded fragments of the Dao Language they were able to comprehend, reproducing each symbol exactly as it appeared within their own resonant understanding.
Every character was the manifestation of a universal law.
A single Dao character could embody concepts that would require entire volumes to express in an ordinary language.
The flow of water. The nature of life and death. The cycle of the seasons. The principle of sharpness. The concept of motion. The essence of flame.
To mortals, such ideas demanded pages of explanation.
To the Dao Language, they could be contained within a single character.
The primer then explained why modern scholars had never succeeded in deciphering it; the symbols are not words. They are living concepts.
A linguist might spend decades studying a particular character and conclude that it meant river.
A cultivator perceiving that same character would understand flow, adaptation, persistence, yielding strength, and the movement of Qi simultaneously.
Neither interpretation was entirely incorrect. Only one was complete.
The Dao Language, the text emphasized, was not read with the eyes. It was read with Qi.
When an ancient cultivator looked upon a Dao character, their Qi resonated with it. The symbol transmitted understanding directly into the mind. The process was neither analytical nor linguistic.
It was experiential.
Stan paused. "So my guess was right."
His voice broke the silence of the dining room.
There almost certainly were surviving cultivation manuals scattered throughout the modern world—in museum collections, archaeological vaults, and the hidden archives of surviving clans.
The reason they had remained useless was suddenly obvious.
Modern humanity lacked Qi. Without Qi, there could be no resonance. Without resonance, there could be no comprehension.
People saw only unfamiliar markings where cultivators perceived living truths. The primer offered an analogy.
It is like presenting a sheet of musical notation to one who has been deaf since birth and asking them to hear the symphony.
The information exists. The medium required to perceive it does not. Stan nodded unconsciously and continued.
The next section described the self-protecting nature of the Dao Language.
A true Dao character could not be reproduced perfectly through ordinary means.
A photograph preserved only its shape, not its essence.
A digital scan captured every line yet lost the intent behind them.
Even a handwritten copy produced by someone incapable of comprehending the Dao became nothing more than an empty imitation, stripped of the resonance that gave the original its meaning.
Only a cultivator who genuinely understood the Dao embodied within the character could reproduce it faithfully.
That, the primer explained, was why the hidden clans had never been overly concerned about cultivation texts leaking into the outside world.
Even if a supreme cultivation manual found its way onto the internet...
Even if millions of people downloaded it...
To ordinary humans, it would remain nothing more than a collection of strange, indecipherable symbols.
To a cultivator with the necessary comprehension, however, that very same manual would be a treasure powerful enough to make ancient nations wage war for its possession.
Stan sat quietly for several moments. That realization settled more heavily than anything else he had read so far.
The system had not merely sold him a language textbook. It had handed him the key to an entire civilization. The ability to read what the modern world could not.
To understand what humanity had forgotten. To unlock libraries of cultivation knowledge that, as far as everyone outside the hidden clans believed, had vanished from history.
He turned the page. The second Chapter began. The real lesson was about to start.
The second Chapter was dense.

The first character introduced was, fittingly, the Dao character for Qi itself, a single, intricate symbol presented across an entire two-page spread, accompanied by a brief but meticulously worded explanation of what it represented, how its component strokes related to one another, and how a practitioner’s own Qi should be guided into resonance with it.
Stan read it carefully. He fixed his attention on the symbol.
For a long moment, nothing happened. He was, in the most literal sense, simply looking at lines of ink on paper.
Then, slowly, so faintly that he almost missed it, a subtle shift rippled through the small reserve of Qi resting in his abdomen.
A gentle current rose from his core, flowed through his chest, and settled behind his eyes.

The character on the page seemed to snap into a second layer of focus he hadn’t realized existed. The strokes that had been nothing more than ink a moment ago now possessed texture. Weight. A faint but unmistakable sense of meaning that he couldn’t articulate, only perceive.
The character meant Qi.

But it also meant breath. And flow. And the connective tissue between all things. And the underlying substrate of existence. And several other concepts that slipped through his grasp the instant he tried to translate them into ordinary language.
It was real. The resonance was real. He spent the next two hours working through the primer.

Over that time, he learned perhaps a dozen Dao characters, Qi, flow, fire, water, earth, mountain, river, life, death, time, void. Each one demanded ten to fifteen minutes of focused study before the resonance settled into place. Once it did, the understanding felt permanent, as though the character had carved itself directly into his mind.
By the end of the session, his thoughts felt saturated.

A soft pressure had formed at the back of his skull, telling him his capacity for this particular kind of learning had, for now, reached its limit. Pushing any further, he instinctively knew, would yield diminishing returns at best and muddled comprehension at worst.
He closed the book. With a thought, he willed it back into his inventory.
It vanished from the table without a trace into the private storage space.
Then he rose to his feet. His shoulders were stiff from spending so long hunched over the book.
He needed to move.
What do you guys think of the story so far?
First, I want to apologize for the info dumps over the last few Chapters. They were necessary to lay the foundation for the new arc we’re about to enter.
I can promise you, though, that this next arc is going to be one of the most exciting yet. Expect more action, higher stakes, and you’ll get to see Stan move in ways you’ve never seen before.

Also, we’ve officially crossed the 300-Chapter milestone! 🎉 I honestly can’t thank you all enough for sticking with the story and supporting it this far. Your comments, reviews, and encouragement have kept me motivated every step of the way.
I promise the story is only going to get even more interesting from here.
New Chapters will be dropping at the usual time tomorrow. See you all then!

chapters.title: Chapter 302: A Pleasant Surprise
paragraphs: He walked into his apartment’s private gym.

The room was exactly as he’d left it that morning, the equipment arranged in neat rows beneath soft, indirect lighting. He hadn’t stepped inside since yesterday’s basketball practice. Between the system upgrades, the Bone-Tempering Pill, the Jade Purity Elixir, dinner with Maya, the rebate cycles, and his study of the Dao Language, the day had simply left no room for exercise.

He walked over to the dumbbell rack. The heaviest pair in the collection weighed two hundred and fifty pounds each, purchased the previous week at his trainer’s suggestion, partly as a joke, partly out of curiosity. Even with his system-enhanced physique, lifting them had once required genuine effort.
He reached down and picked one up. He nearly threw it. Not because it was too heavy. Because it wasn’t.

The two-hundred-and-fifty-pound dumbbell felt almost weightless in his hand. He could feel the cool steel beneath his fingers, the texture of the knurled grip, even the inertia of the metal as he moved it, but the crushing pull of gravity that should have accompanied its mass simply wasn’t there.
It was like holding a foam prop shaped to resemble a dumbbell.
Stan stared at it for a long moment. Then he slowly curled it. He did it effortlessly...
He lowered it just as smoothly before extending his arm straight out in front of him. Still effortless. Like he was lifting a feather...
He rotated his wrist in slow circles, holding the weight fully extended. His shoulder didn’t tremble. His forearm didn’t tighten. It felt as though he could maintain the position indefinitely.
He lowered the dumbbell and picked up its partner.
One in each hand. Five hundred pounds in total, still nothing.
"...Sigh." The word escaped him as he looked at the pair of dumbbells. "What use is this gym room now..."

The Bone-Tempering Pill had increased the density of his skeleton by roughly fivefold. The Jade Purity Elixir had refined every other aspect of his body to near-perfect efficiency, while the Qi now circulating through his meridians reinforced every movement he made.
The combined effect was absurd. The level of strength he’d considered exceptional that morning had become almost meaningless by evening.
He set the dumbbells back onto the rack and walked over to the loaded barbell.
Before today’s transformations, he’d been deadlifting around eight hundred pounds, close to the upper limit of what his enhanced body had been capable of.
He bent down, wrapped his hands around the bar, and lifted.
The weight rose as effortlessly as if it were an empty training bar.
He set it back down, straightened, then slowly shook his head.
"So this is what that pill did," he murmured. "Still feels surreal."
He didn’t bother testing his limits.

There was little point. He was already reasonably certain the equipment would reach its maximum capacity long before he reached his own. Based on what he’d just experienced, even a conservative estimate placed his current physical strength at nearly ten times what it had been that morning.
Leaving the weight rack behind, he walked over to the treadmill.
He set it to a comfortable running pace and started moving.
He didn’t need the exercise. His cardiovascular system was almost certainly operating at a level no conventional training program could meaningfully improve.
But the rhythmic motion helped. After two hours spent immersing himself in the Dao Language, he wanted something simple. Familiar. A chance to let his mind settle while his body moved on instinct.
He ran for fifteen minutes at an easy pace.

As the treadmill hummed beneath his feet, he watched the lights of the city glitter beyond the floor-to-ceiling windows. His thoughts drifted over everything the evening had brought, the rebates, the inventory, the Dao Language, and the staggering new baseline of his physical abilities.
Then his phone rang. It rested on the side table beside the treadmill.
He stepped off the moving belt, walked over, and picked it up.
The caller ID displayed a familiar name.
[Sarah.]
A faint smile touched his lips as he swiped to answer.
"Sarah."
"Surprise!"

Her voice came through bright and warm, carrying that unmistakable, giddy lilt she always had whenever she was pleased with herself over some small private mischief. Behind her, he caught the sound of wind and the faint echo of footsteps on tile.
"What are you up to?"
"Oh, nothing. Bye."
The line went dead.
She had hung up.
Stan stared at the phone for a moment, one eyebrow lifting.
"...Okay."
Then, almost on cue, the doorbell chimed.
A clean, gentle sound echoed through the apartment. Understanding dawned instantly.
A slow, effortless smile spread across his face, the quiet smile of a man who had just been pleasantly outmaneuvered.
He set the phone back on the table, left the gym, crossed the hallway, and opened the front door.
Sarah stood on the doorstep.

An overnight bag rested at her feet. In one hand, she carried a takeaway bag that smelled unmistakably of something homemade, warm, savory, and infused with fresh herbs. She wore a soft cream knit sweater that draped loosely past her hips, dark jeans, and the small gold pendant he had given her a few weeks earlier, glinting at the open collar. Her hair fell freely over her shoulders, her makeup was light, and she looked exactly like a woman who had decided hours ago that she was going to surprise him and had stubbornly refused to second-guess herself ever since.
She lifted her chin, meeting his eyes.
"Surprise," she repeated, this time more softly.
Stan leaned against the doorframe, his smile widening.
"What a surprise."
"You’ve forgotten all about me, Stan."
"I promise I haven’t." He tapped the side of his head. "You’re still up here."
Then he rested a hand lightly against his chest.
"And in here."
Sarah tried to look offended, though the corners of her lips were already betraying her.
"Well... it’s been so long that I figured I’d come and see you myself. Your apartment isn’t exactly a secret." She tilted her head. "So... are you going to let me in?"
Stan pretended to consider it.
"I’m thinking about it."
"Stan."
She puffed out her cheeks in an exaggerated pout.
He chuckled, stepped aside, and pulled the door fully open.
"Come in."

She picked up her overnight bag and walked past him into the apartment, the takeaway bag swaying gently at her side. As she brushed by, she left behind the comforting aroma of a meal she had clearly spent hours preparing.
Stan watched her for a moment before closing the door behind them.

chapters.title: Chapter 303: Missed You
paragraphs: Sarah stepped deeper into the apartment, her eyes sweeping over the familiar space with quiet affection.
She set the takeaway bag on the marble kitchen island and placed her overnight bag beside the couch, moving with the easy comfort of someone who already felt at home here.
Stan opened the fridge and pulled out a chilled bottle of sparkling lemonade, pouring two glasses. He slid one across the island to her.
"Sadly, this and water is all I have right now," he said with a small, apologetic smile. "I haven’t had a chance to restock."

Sarah’s eyes crinkled with warmth. She picked up the glass, took a sip, then pointed at the fragrant takeaway bag. "It’s a good thing I brought this, then. Homemade braised short ribs, garlic mashed potatoes, and roasted vegetables. I spent the whole afternoon in the kitchen thinking about you." She gave him a soft, teasing look. "Figured you’d forget to eat properly again."

Stan rounded the island and drew her close with one arm. He leaned in and pressed a gentle, lingering peck to her cheek, his lips brushing warmly against her skin. The faint scent of her shampoo, something light and floral, filled his senses.
"Mmm," he murmured against her cheek. "Give me a few minutes. I’m coming to join you. Just want to wash the day off."
Sarah turned her head slightly, catching his lips in a quick, sweet kiss before he could pull away. "Take your time. I’ll set the table."
He lingered for a second longer, forehead resting against hers, then headed toward the bathroom with a reluctant smile.

Fifteen minutes later, Stan returned wearing a simple black t-shirt and soft lounge pants, his hair still slightly damp. The apartment smelled even better now, Sarah had warmed the food. With soft ambient music playing in the background, it felt very romantic.
They ate slowly, legs occasionally brushing under the table. Between bites, Sarah kept stealing glances at him, her expression soft and open.

"I missed you," she said quietly after a while, setting her fork down. Her voice carried a vulnerable honesty that made his chest tighten. "I know you’ve been busy with... everything. After that last time I’ve kept thinking about you wondering when I’d get to spend time with you again."

Stan reached across the table and took her hand, his thumb stroking gently over her knuckles. "I missed you too. More than I realized until I heard your voice on the phone. Even with all the changes happening to me... this, being with you, still feels like the most important part of my day."

chapters.title: Chapter 304: Crunchy
paragraphs: Meanwhile, in an endless snowfield stretched beneath the night.
The frozen plain ran flat and pale to the horizon, broken only by the slow rise and fall of drifts sculpted by countless storms.
Above, the sky had deepened into a vast indigo, the last traces of daylight swallowed behind distant mountains, and the cold settled over the land like an immense, invisible weight.
Loose snow hissed across the hard-packed surface, dry as sand, streaming in long white ribbons that twisted, scattered, and formed anew with every restless gust.
Far away, jagged peaks stood in silent ranks, their shoulders draped in snow, their dark faces swallowed by shadow.
Nothing moved. Nothing lived. Only the wind, endless, patient, and relentless, scraped across a world of ice.
And in the heart of that frozen emptiness, a single fire burned.
It was a stubborn orange flame, crouched low against the wind, casting a tight circle of warmth that held the darkness at bay for only a few precious feet.

Sparks burst free from the fire, racing sideways before vanishing into the night. Its flickering light washed over the faces gathered around it in shifting gold, while beyond them the darkness pressed close, so complete that the men seemed cradled within a lone pocket of warmth in an otherwise endless wilderness.
There were six of them, wrapped in heavy furs, their beards rimed with frost.
And they were happy.

The day’s kill turned slowly over the flames, its steaming carcass dripping fat that hissed and snapped as it struck the glowing coals. The rich scent of roasted meat filled the air before the wind stole it away into the frozen night. One of the hunters rotated the spit with a gloved hand, tore off a strip of meat, and hissed as the heat bit into his fingers. He tossed it from palm to palm before finally taking a hearty bite. Grease glistened in his beard.
He muttered something through a full mouth.
The man beside him burst into laughter, the sound booming into the stillness as white breath billowed from his lips. He clapped the hunter hard enough on the shoulder to make him stumble.
"Eat slower," another called. "You’ll choke, and then who’s carrying the hides?"
"Better choking than freezing."
The fire crackled.

Someone passed around a skin filled with something far stronger than water. It traveled from hand to hand, each man taking a long pull before exhaling sharply, grinning as warmth spread through his chest. Their voices overlapped in easy conversation, the relaxed banter of men who had worked hard, hunted well, and earned a quiet night beneath the open sky. The hunt had been successful. The kill had been clean. Tomorrow they would return home with packs heavy with meat.
Tonight, they had fire.
Food.
And one another.
For now, that was enough.
The youngest among them animatedly recounted a story, punctuating every sentence with broad gestures while the others interrupted with jokes and jeers. Firelight danced in their eyes.
Then one of them stopped laughing.
His gaze drifted beyond the circle of firelight, into the vast darkness where the snow stretched away without end.
The warmth left his face.
He narrowed his eyes and leaned forward ever so slightly, as though straining to catch sight of something hidden beyond the reach of the flames.
Out there, far beyond the firelight, at the very edge of where the eye could reach, there were shapes.

Small. Dark. Three of them, perhaps four, standing in a loose row against the endless white. So distant they were little more than smudges, upright marks on the snow, the sort of thing that could have been rocks, stunted trees, or simply tricks of weary eyes and failing light.
Except there were no rocks out there. No trees. Nothing. And they were standing perfectly, unnaturally still.
"Is that a," he began, his voice coming out thinner than he intended.
"Sit down," one of the others said without even looking. "It’s snow. A drift. You’ve had too much of that skin."
"Drink your drink, ghost-hunter."

Laughter followed, quieter this time. A few of the men glanced toward the horizon, more to indulge him than out of concern. The fire crackled. The wind swept a curtain of loose snow between the camp and the distant shapes, blurring them into wavering shadows.
"There’s nothing," one of the hunters started, finally turning to look properly.
The shapes were gone. No. They were here.
There was no crossing of the distance. No figures growing larger as they ran over the snow. One blink, they stood a thousand yards away at the rim of the world.

The next, firelight washed across grey fur slick with frost, long wet fangs, and eyes that caught the flames and hurled the gold back at them. Close enough to touch. Close enough that the heat of the fire illuminated the steam rising from their hides.
No one screamed. Everything happened so fast... It ended in the space between two heartbeats.
Most of those hearts never reached the second.

A blur of grey tore through the circle, and a man simply came apart, his upper half flung one way while the rest of him remained where he had been sitting. Another vanished beneath something enormous, the impact kicking the fire sideways in an explosion of sparks that scattered across the snow.

Wet tearing sounds came one after another in savage succession. A weapon spun into the darkness from fingers no longer attached to an arm. Someone folded backward across the glowing coals. The youngest hunter’s story died in his throat before it could become a scream.
And then... Silence.
The wind continued as it always had, hissing loose snow over the frozen crust with complete indifference.

The fire, half scattered from its bed, crackled weakly now, its diminished glow casting long crimson shadows across the torn earth. The comforting scent of roasting meat still lingered in the air, now tainted by something hotter.
Sharper. Copper-rich... Blood.

It spread slowly across the snow in dark, branching fingers, soaking into the white until crimson blossoms bloomed where moments before there had been only untouched frost. Thin wisps of steam curled upward wherever it pooled.
Separate streams met, merged, and widened until the entire campsite became a ruin of scarlet and churned slush, while beyond it the snow remained flawless all the way to the horizon.
A severed head rolled across the frozen ground, slow and uneven, before coming to rest against a drift. Firelight flickered in its open, unseeing eyes.
A weapon lay half-buried nearby, its edge catching the dying glow.
Scattered furs. A split wineskin, its dark contents spreading across the snow before freezing into the ice.
The embers pulsed a dull orange beneath the churned slush. Fading and fading.
And in the silence, new sounds emerged; the wet, deliberate tearing of flesh, the sharp crack of bone giving way between powerful jaws. A low, contented hum, almost a sigh.

Off to one side, one of the great grey beasts sat back on its haunches, patient, its long muzzle tilted toward the sky. Across the clearing, a severed head came tumbling through the firelit air, spinning end over end, flung loose in the frenzy of feeding. It traced a slow, lazy arc before dropping neatly into the creature’s waiting jaws.
Its mouth closed.
CRUNCH
The werewolf chewed slowly, unhurriedly, working its jaws with the care of something savoring a taste long forgotten. It rolled the morsel across its tongue. Its eyes drifted half shut.
"Crunchy," it murmured, its deep voice thick and oddly gentle. "It’s been so long."

The others never looked up. They were already feeding, great grey forms hunched over the mangled bodies, speaking between mouthfuls the way men might converse around a dinner table, easy, familiar, with all the patience in the world.
"After tens of centuries," one said without raising its head, "we’re finally out."
Another tore something free with a wet wrench of muscle and sinew. It paused only long enough to swallow before replying.
"I can finally eat human flesh in peace." It let out a satisfied breath. "Those True Humans were troublesome."
A low rumble of agreement answered from somewhere in the circle. Another bone splintered.
The wind drew a ribbon of loose snow through the ruined camp. The scattered embers glowed one final, weary crimson before surrendering to darkness.
Above them, the mountains loomed black against the deep indigo sky.
The snowfield stretched away, flat, silent, and endless in every direction.
And at its center, the ancient things bent over their feast, unhurried, content and free.

chapters.title: Chapter 305: Antarctica
paragraphs: After a good night rest with Sarah, Stan woke slowly.

Morning light had already begun filtering through the bedroom curtains by the time consciousness fully returned. Sarah was still asleep against his shoulder, her breathing soft and even, her hair fanned across the pillow and spilling over his arm. The overnight bag she’d brought rested at the foot of the bed, now unpacked and neatly rearranged, a small domestic detail that suggested she’d decided, sometime during the night, to settle in comfortably and make herself at home.
For a few quiet moments, he simply held her, reluctant to disturb the peaceful stillness of the morning.
Eventually, he shifted, and she stirred with him. She blinked awake, smiled sleepily, and they eased into the gentle rituals of a shared morning.

They lingered together in the large bathtub, the water warm and soothing, the bath less about getting clean than about enjoying each other’s company. Sarah washed his shoulders with slow, absent-minded care while he helped rinse the shampoo from her hair.

Their conversation drifted effortlessly from one ordinary subject to another. She told him about her sister’s engagement, the new shipment of dresses arriving at the boutique on Steel Street, and a few amusing incidents that had unfolded at work during the week. He listened with quiet interest, occasionally teasing her, occasionally asking questions, content simply to hear her talk.
When they were dressed, Stan drove her home in the Audi.

He walked her to the entrance of her building, kissed her once before she went inside, and watched as she disappeared through the lobby doors, offering him one last warm, contented wave over her shoulder.
Only then did he return to the car and drive back toward Aurelia Heights.
He settled at the dining table with a fresh cup of coffee and opened his laptop.
At the back of his mind lingered the final thread from Introduction to Earth.
’Antarctica.’
The book’s closing sentence had been deliberately crafted to point him there.
Before letting the system lead him any further, he wanted to see what he could uncover on his own. So he opened his guugle browser, navigated to a news aggregator, and began scrolling.
He found it within thirty seconds.

The story dominated nearly every science and general-interest feed. Its headline was restrained, precisely the kind of measured language reputable science journalists used when reporting on a discovery that was extraordinary but not yet fully understood.
[Antarctic Researcher Discovers Unclassified Liquid Pool Beneath Glacier, Substance Defies Known Chemistry]
Stan set his coffee down and clicked.
The article was comprehensive, published by a respected scientific news outlet, it was three days old...

The researcher at its center was Dr. Halvard Sigurdsson, a renowned glaciologist and Antarctic scientist with more than two decades of polar field experience and a reputation for cautious, methodical work. The report opened with an overview of the discovery before transitioning into lengthy excerpts from a joint press conference he had given two days earlier.
As Stan read on, the implications became increasingly difficult to ignore.

During what had begun as a routine glacial survey in a remote sector of Antarctica’s interior, Sigurdsson and his team had uncovered a subterranean pool of liquid that, by every accepted scientific model, should not have existed.

«"It is not water," Sigurdsson said during the conference. "That was the first conclusion we reached, and I want to be absolutely clear about that. The substance remains liquid at temperatures well below the freezing point of any known aqueous solution. We recorded ambient conditions that should have solidified every liquid currently recognized by modern chemistry. This material did not freeze. It did not become more viscous. It exhibited none of the transitional behavior we associate with a liquid approaching its freezing point. It simply remained... liquid."»
The article went on to describe the substance’s physical properties.

It was perfectly transparent, so clear that the team had initially mistaken it for exceptionally pure water reflecting the surrounding ice. Yet its measured density failed to correspond with any known liquid catalogued in international scientific databases. Its viscosity fluctuated unpredictably under repeated testing, while its refractive index fell outside every established reference range.
Even more perplexing were the results of its chemical analysis.

Multiple spectroscopic scans had produced essentially nothing. The instruments consistently returned null or unreadable data, as though the substance possessed no recognizable molecular or elemental signature. Despite repeated calibrations and the use of different analytical techniques, the researchers were unable to identify a single component that fit within any existing chemical framework.
But it was the liquid’s behavior, not its composition, that had propelled the discovery into headlines around the world.
According to the report, the substance dissolved almost everything that came into contact with it.

Sigurdsson’s team had attempted to collect samples using every container available to them. Stainless steel vessels dissolved within seconds. Glass containers disintegrated even faster. Specialized polymer canisters softened and liquefied in ways the researchers described as chemically impossible. Stone samples vanished into the liquid. Ordinary ice dissolved almost immediately. Even biological tissue, tested under tightly controlled laboratory conditions using animal specimens, broke down within moments of exposure.
Every attempt to retrieve a sample ended the same way.
The container was destroyed before it could be removed.
But one detail stood apart from all the others.
The glacier itself remained completely unaffected.

The walls of the cavity containing the pool showed no measurable erosion. No pitting. No signs of chemical reaction whatsoever. The liquid rested inside a perfectly stable chamber, dissolving virtually every known material that touched it,
except the ancient ice that enclosed it.
Sigurdsson concluded the press conference with a statement that had already begun circulating across scientific circles and social media alike for its remarkable restraint.

«"We cannot explain this. Our current chemical models are inadequate. The substance represents either an unknown chemical compound, a previously undiscovered phase of matter, or a material formed under conditions that have never before been observed on Earth. Further investigation is required."»

The article closed by noting that the announcement had sparked intense international interest over the previous forty-eight hours. Governments, universities, and research institutions around the world had already begun coordinating efforts to study the phenomenon.
Stan read the article a second time.
Slowly, he set his coffee on the table.
Then he leaned back in his chair.
’Antarctica.’
The system had directed him toward Antarctica.
Two days earlier, one of the world’s leading glaciologists had announced the discovery of a substance that appeared to defy the foundations of modern chemistry.
The connection wasn’t subtle.
It was practically pointing at him.

chapters.title: Chapter 306: Spirit Pool: The Path of Immortality Begins
paragraphs: At that moment, the system responded.
[Ding!]
[Anomalous phenomenon detected. Cross-referencing with host’s environment.]
[Initializing System Scan.]
[Scanning Earth...]
Stan straightened in his chair.
"...You can do that?"

Until this moment, the system had never hinted at possessing anything resembling a planetary scanning capability. He had assumed its awareness was limited to his immediate surroundings and the people directly connected to him.
Apparently, he had underestimated it.
By a considerable margin.
The system ignored his question and continued.
[Scan in progress.]
[Priority target: substances exhibiting Qi resonance.]
[Estimated completion time: several minutes.]
Stan stared at the glowing text.
"...Qi resonance."
Before he could process that phrase, another notification appeared.
[Preliminary result: Cure for host’s meridian obstruction detected.]
He frowned.
"My what?"
A second notification immediately followed.
[Preliminary result: Spirit Pool identified.]
Stan sat upright.
"Wait."
He stared at the words for a long moment before speaking again.
"Meridian obstruction? What meridian obstruction? I have a meridian obstruction?"
The system answered without hesitation.
[Confirmed, host.]

[Your meridian network is structurally complete but partially obstructed at its intake pathways. While your meridians are capable of generating, circulating, and expelling Qi, they are unable to absorb ambient Qi from the external environment.]

[The Bone-Tempering Pill and Jade Purity Elixir introduced a limited reserve of Qi into your body, allowing basic circulation and utilization. However, without functional intake pathways, your internal reserves cannot be replenished naturally.]
Stan frowned. "So, my body’s running on a battery with no charger.
[Analogy accepted.]

[Prior to recent events, this condition carried no practical disadvantage. Since the Great Withering, Earth’s ambient Qi has remained effectively nonexistent. The sudden abnormal introduction to qi caused an inability to absorb external Qi which resulted in immeasurable loss of function of the meridians connecting your pores to your dantian.]
The next message appeared after a brief pause.
[The emergence of the Spirit Pool beneath the Antarctic glacier indicates that this environmental condition may be changing.]
[Ambient Qi may be returning to Earth.]
Stan sat motionless for a long moment.
The implications of the system’s revelations were staggering.
For the past few hours, ever since he read introduction to earth, he’d assumed the reason he hadn’t pursued Qi cultivation was simple: there was no Qi left to cultivate.

Introduction to Earth had explained that well, following the Night of Vanishing, the world’s Qi had gradually faded until it was all but extinct. He’d taken that to mean no one, not even himself, could absorb it because there simply wasn’t any.
While that was true he also had a problem himself;

His meridians were intact, but the pathways responsible for drawing Qi into his body were partially obstructed. Even if Earth had been overflowing with spiritual energy, he still wouldn’t have been able to absorb a single thread of it.
The Bone-Tempering Pill and the Jade Purity Elixir had given him a finite reserve of Qi, enough to circulate and use.
But once that reserve was exhausted,
That would be it.
No replenishment.
No further cultivation.
Which meant that if ambient Qi truly was returning to Earth, as the system now believed, it would change nothing for him until his obstruction was removed.

And the cure, apparently, was sitting inside a pool of impossible liquid beneath an Antarctic glacier, a pool that had become the most talked-about scientific discovery on the planet less than forty-eight hours earlier.
The system interrupted his thoughts.
[Earth scan continuing...]
A second notification appeared almost immediately.
[Discovery: Active Divine Formation.]
Stan barely had time to wonder what a Divine Formation was before another line replaced it.
[Discovery: Dormant Realm Portal.]
"...A what?"
No explanation came. Instead, the notifications continued.
[Constructing dynamic geographical map of Earth.]
[Spirit Pool coordinates integrated.]
[Additional locations of interest will be added as further discoveries are confirmed.]
A final series of windows appeared.
[Mission acquired.]
[Objective: Acquire the map. Retrieve the cure and embark upon the path of immortality.]
[Time Limit: Seven days, or until the Spirit Pool is claimed by another party, whichever occurs first.]
Stan stared at the words. ’The path of immortality huh?’
This is all crazy, the phrase was so wildly disconnected from the reality of his morning that he almost laughed.
He was sitting at the dining table of his apartment in Aurelia Heights, drinking a flat white while reading the news on his laptop.
And now his system was calmly informing him that a chemically impossible pool beneath an Antarctic glacier was the first milestone on the road to immortality.
With a deadline. Seven days. He closed his eyes and rubbed his temples.
At some point, he was going to have to accept that his understanding of reality required frequent updates.
Taking a slow breath, he focused inward.
"The Spirit Pool." He paused. "That’s the cure?"
[Correct, host.]
"How much does the map cost?"
[Ten System Points.]
Stan checked his balance. His account still held approximately one hundred and twenty billion dollars.
At the current exchange rate, that translated to one hundred and twenty System Points.
Ten was insignificant. Without hesitation, he initiated the conversion. Ten billion dollars vanished from his bank account.
His System Point balance increased by ten. He spent them immediately.
[Purchase confirmed.]
[World Map successfully integrated into host’s perceptual field.]
Stan blinked. His vision shifted almost imperceptibly.
A small, luminous arrow materialized in the upper-right corner of his peripheral vision. It was subtle enough not to obstruct his sight, yet impossible to ignore. The arrow pointed steadily south.
He focused on it.
Instantly, it unfolded into a three-dimensional projection suspended within his mind’s eye.

A complete rendering of Earth rotated silently before him, its continents and oceans reproduced with breathtaking precision. Clouds drifted across the atmosphere. Weather systems spiraled over the seas. The globe possessed the clarity of a high-resolution satellite model, yet felt somehow more alive than any digital map he’d ever seen.
Near the frozen heart of Antarctica, a single point of brilliant light pulsed steadily.
The Spirit Pool. With another thought, the projection collapsed. The globe vanished.
The arrow returned to its quiet place at the edge of his vision, continuing to point toward the Antarctic continent.
Stan gave a slow, thoughtful nod.
"...That’s going to be incredibly useful."

chapters.title: Chapter 307: When The Shadows Stir
paragraphs: Another thought came to Stan at that moment...

If the discovery of the Spirit Pool had truly gone viral over the past forty-eight hours, then the global scientific community was already aware of it. And if scientists knew, then governments, research institutions, and private laboratories certainly did as well.
By now, plans would already be in motion. Expeditions. Funding approvals. Access negotiations. Sample retrieval missions and test..
The international race to investigate the anomaly had almost certainly begun.
But the system hadn’t warned him that the scientific community might reach the Spirit Pool first.
It had warned him that it could be claimed by another party.
That wording was deliberate. Which meant the real competition probably wasn’t ordinary scientists.
Stan’s thoughts drifted back to Introduction to Earth.
The hidden clans. Ancient cultivation lineages that had survived the Night of Vanishing by withdrawing from public history and allowing themselves to become little more than myths.
If they still existed, and everything he’d experienced suggested they did, then they would recognize the Spirit Pool for what it truly was long before any modern laboratory could.
To the scientific world, it was an inexplicable chemical anomaly.
To cultivators, it was a treasure.

If those hidden clans had preserved even a fraction of their former knowledge, the appearance of a Spirit Pool would have sent shockwaves through every secret organization still watching the world from the shadows.
Which meant the countdown wasn’t really against governments or research teams.
It was against people who already understood exactly what they were looking at.
He needed to know how much the public knew.
More importantly, he needed to know what wasn’t being reported.
Stan reached for his phone and called Amelia.
She picked up on the first ring.
"Stan."
"Amelia, I need a favor."
"Go ahead."

"I need Vanguard to tap its intelligence network and assess the current landscape surrounding the Antarctic liquid pool discovery. I don’t care about the public narrative. I want to know who’s actually paying attention, not the people giving interviews, but the ones quietly moving money, equipment, and personnel."
There was a brief silence.
"...That’s a very specific request."
"I know, that’s why I need the vanguard."
"I’ll call you back."
The line went dead. Thirty-two minutes later, his phone rang. Stan answered immediately.
"Amelia."
"Stan." There was a tautness in her voice that hadn’t been there before. "You were right to ask."
His expression sharpened.
"Tell me."
"The public conversation is exactly what you’d expect. Scientists are debating the chemistry. Universities are requesting access. Journalists are publishing analyses. That’s the visible layer."
"And underneath?"
A short pause.
"Underneath, it’s something else entirely."
She continued.
"The organizations mobilizing serious resources toward Antarctica aren’t primarily scientific institutions.
Stan remained silent.
"They’re being funded."
"By whom?"
"Old-money family offices."
She let the words hang between them.

"The funding started appearing within the last forty-eight hours. Shell companies are suddenly underwriting polar expeditions, chartering specialized transport, acquiring cold-weather equipment, and leasing logistics vessels. On paper, it looks like private investment in scientific research."
"But it isn’t."
"No."
"What do the ownership trails show?"
"When our analysts dug through the corporate layers, they kept arriving at the same destination."
She exhaled quietly. "Families."
"What kind of families?"
"The kind that have been wealthy for centuries."
Stan’s eyes narrowed.

"Vanguard tracked at least a dozen private aircraft filing flight plans toward South American staging points over the past twenty-four hours. Most are registered to corporate proxies, but the beneficial ownership traces back to family offices with no previous involvement in polar research."
"And they’re all moving now?"
"Almost simultaneously."
She didn’t need to say the obvious.
That kind of coordination didn’t happen by accident.
"This isn’t a scientific response," Amelia said quietly. "It’s organized. Deliberate. And remarkably discreet."
Stan leaned back in his chair. "Thank you."
"You expected this?"
"Yes, I was hoping I was wrong."
"What exactly were you expecting?"
He was silent for a moment. "I’ll explain when I get back."
"...Get back from where?"
"Antarctica."
Silence. Then—
"Stan."
"I have to go."
"Why?"
"It’s important."
"Important enough to fly to Antarctica on almost no notice?"
"Yes."
Another pause.
"How long?
"A few days." He considered it. "Ten at the absolute most."
Amelia sighed. "...All right."
Her tone softened. "Be careful."
She hesitated before continuing. "If these families are moving this aggressively, then whatever they’re after isn’t something ordinary people are supposed to find."
"I know."
"I mean it, Stan."
"I’ll be careful."
"If you need anything, transport, equipment, legal cover, personnel, emergency extraction, Vanguard has assets almost everywhere."
A faint smile crossed his face. "I’ll let you know."
"You’d better."
Another brief silence.
Then she spoke more quietly. "Come back."
"I will."
The call ended.
Stan continued holding the phone for several seconds before lowering it onto the table.
The confirmation was exactly what he’d feared.
The old families were moving. Which meant the hidden world, or whatever remained of it, hadn’t merely noticed the Spirit Pool.
They had recognized it. And they had begun mobilizing almost immediately.
The system’s seven-day deadline suddenly felt far less generous.
A faint smile tugged at the corner of his mouth.
"As expected." He leaned back, thinking aloud. "So cultivation knowledge isn’t entirely lost."
His gaze drifted toward the window.
"Those families almost certainly know exactly what a Spirit Pool is."
He fell silent.
Then another, far more practical realization struck him.
"...How am I actually supposed to get to Antarctica?"
He had the money. That wasn’t the problem. He didn’t own an aircraft capable of making the journey. Even if he did, he couldn’t fly one.
He had no experience navigating Antarctic logistics, securing landing permissions, or arranging transport onto one of the most isolated continents on Earth.
Unlimited wealth solved many problems. But it didn’t automatically solve this one. The thought had barely finished forming before—
Before the thought had fully formed, the system answered.
[Host concern detected.]
[Analyzing viable solutions...]
[Shop Updating...]
[Shop update complete.]
[New category unlocked: Skill & Profession Mastery.]
[Recommended purchase: Advanced Pilot Mastery.]
[Cost: 10 System Points.]
Stan blinked. Then he laughed. It was a quiet, disbelieving laugh.

"When our analysts dug through the corporate layers, they kept arriving at the same destination."
She exhaled quietly.
"Families."
"What kind of families?"
"The kind that have been wealthy for centuries."
Stan’s eyes narrowed.
"Vanguard tracked at least a dozen private aircraft filing flight plans toward South American staging points over the past twenty-four hours.
Most are registered to corporate proxies, but the beneficial ownership traces back to family offices with no previous involvement in polar research."
"And they’re all moving now?"
"Almost simultaneously."
She didn’t need to say the obvious.
That kind of coordination didn’t happen by accident.
"This isn’t a scientific response," Amelia said quietly.
"It’s organized.
Deliberate.
And remarkably discreet."
Stan leaned back in his chair.
"Thank you."
"You expected this?"
"Yes, I was hoping I was wrong."
"What exactly were you expecting?"
He was silent for a moment.
"I’ll explain when I get back."
"...Get back from where?"
"Antarctica."
Silence.
Then—
"Stan."
"I have to go."
"Why?"
"It’s important."
"Important enough to fly to Antarctica on almost no notice?"
"Yes."
Another pause.
"How long?
"A few days." He considered it.
"Ten at the absolute most."
Amelia sighed.
"...All right."
Her tone softened.
"Be careful."
She hesitated before continuing.
"If these families are moving this aggressively, then whatever they’re after isn’t something ordinary people are supposed to find."
"I know."
"I mean it, Stan."
"I’ll be careful."
"If you need anything, transport, equipment, legal cover, personnel, emergency extraction, Vanguard has assets almost everywhere."
A faint smile crossed his face.
"I’ll let you know."
"You’d better."
Another brief silence.
Then she spoke more quietly.
"Come back."
"I will."
The call ended.
Stan continued holding the phone for several seconds before lowering it onto the table.
The confirmation was exactly what he’d feared.
The old families were moving.
Which meant the hidden world, or whatever remained of it, hadn’t merely noticed the Spirit Pool.
They had recognized it.
And they had begun mobilizing almost immediately.
The system’s seven-day deadline suddenly felt far less generous.
A faint smile tugged at the corner of his mouth.
"As expected." He leaned back, thinking aloud.
"So cultivation knowledge isn’t entirely lost."
His gaze drifted toward the window.
"Those families almost certainly know exactly what a Spirit Pool is."
He fell silent.
Then another, far more practical realization struck him.
"...How am I actually supposed to get to Antarctica?"
He had the money.
That wasn’t the problem.
He didn’t own an aircraft capable of making the journey.
Even if he did, he couldn’t fly one.
He had no experience navigating Antarctic logistics, securing landing permissions, or arranging transport onto one of the most isolated continents on Earth.
Unlimited wealth solved many problems.
But it didn’t automatically solve this one.
The thought had barely finished forming before—
Before the thought had fully formed, the system answered.
[Host concern detected.]
[Analyzing viable solutions...]
[Shop Updating...]
[Shop update complete.]
[New category unlocked: Skill & Profession Mastery.]
[Recommended purchase: Advanced Pilot Mastery.]
[Cost: 10 System Points.]
Stan blinked.
Then he laughed.
It was a quiet, disbelieving laugh.

chapters.title: Chapter 308: First Flight: The Sky Is The First Gate
paragraphs: [Recommended purchase: Advanced Pilot Mastery.]
[Cost: 10 System Points.]
Stan blinked. Then he laughed. It was a quiet, disbelieving laugh.

Apparently, the system didn’t just respond to his actions, it anticipated his practical problems and expanded its capabilities to solve them. He’d wondered, for all of three seconds, how he was supposed to fly himself to Antarctica.
The system had calmly added pilot training to the shop.
He opened the newly unlocked category.
[SKILL & PROFESSION MASTERY]
The list was enormous. Profession-grade knowledge packages ranged from three to fifteen System Points, neatly organized into broad disciplines.
Combat. Vehicle Operation. Craftsmanship. Medicine. Engineering. Analytical Sciences. Languages & Culture... And many more.
Each category expanded into dozens of specialized disciplines.
Stan scrolled through them with growing fascination.
The realization slowly settled over him. The system wasn’t merely selling information. It was selling experience.
Years. Decades. Entire careers, distilled into purchasable knowledge that could be integrated directly into his mind.
He converted another ten billion dollars into ten System Points without hesitation.
Then he purchased [Advanced Pilot Mastery.]
[Purchase confirmed.]
[Advanced Pilot Mastery successfully integrated.]
Knowledge poured into his mind, not as a chaotic torrent, but as an impossibly organized expansion of memory.
Aerodynamics. Aircraft systems. Meteorology. Air traffic communication. Instrument flight. Emergency procedures. Fuel planning. Long-range navigation. Polar operations. Cold-weather aviation.

He instinctively understood the cockpit layouts of commercial airliners, turboprops, helicopters, and long-range business jets. Checklists that had never existed in his memory suddenly felt as familiar as his own name. Complex procedures unfolded in his thoughts with effortless clarity, as though he had spent decades flying every major aircraft certification required for civilian aviation.
The integration ended as quietly as it had begun.
Stan let out a slow breath.
If someone handed him the keys to a private jet at this very moment, he could fly it. Confidently and safely.
His thoughts shifted. Antarctica wasn’t simply remote. It was dangerous.

Amelia’s intelligence report had all but confirmed that powerful organizations were already converging on the Spirit Pool. If the hidden families truly understood what it was, then there was every possibility he would encounter resistance.
His body was already extraordinary.
The Bone-Tempering Pill had transformed his physique beyond human limits.
But raw strength and genuine combat mastery were two very different things.
At present, his fighting ability amounted to little more than good instincts and the experience of surviving the streets.
Against trained opponents, that wouldn’t be enough.
He opened the Combat category. Several packages appeared.
Boxing Mastery. Grappling Mastery. Advanced Blade Mastery. Advanced Firearms Mastery.
His eyes stopped at the first listing. It cost more than any other skill in the category.
[Martial Arts Grand Mastery.]
[Comprehensive mastery of armed and unarmed combat across all major martial disciplines.]
[Cost: 15 System Points.]
He smiled. "Seems worthwhile."
Another fifteen billion dollars disappeared from his account. The purchase completed instantly.
[Purchase confirmed.]
[Martial Arts Grand Mastery successfully integrated.]

This time, the knowledge felt different. It didn’t simply add information. It rewrote instinct. Countless forms, techniques, and principles unfolded within his consciousness, layering themselves over the strength his transformed body already possessed.
Footwork. Balance. Timing. Distance. Momentum. Joint manipulation. Weapon transitions. Spatial awareness.
Every strike, throw, lock, feint, and counter became second nature.
His muscles seemed to remember movements they had never performed.
His posture shifted almost imperceptibly. His breathing settled.
Even sitting perfectly still, he carried the effortless composure of someone who had spent a lifetime refining violence into an art.
The integration faded. Stan remained seated for several long moments, silently absorbing the enormity of what had just happened.
Less than a minute earlier, he’d been an exceptionally strong man.
Now, he possessed the technical foundation of a grandmaster who had devoted multiple lifetimes to the study of combat.
Satisfied, he reached for his phone.
There was one more call he needed to make.
He dialed Grayson.
Grayson answered on the second ring. "Stan."
"Grayson, I need you to acquire a long-range private jet."
A brief pause.
"What kind of jet?"
"Something capable of true intercontinental range. It needs to be able to operate on polar routes, including flights to Antarctica."
Silence. Then—
"...I’m sorry, Stan. Could you repeat that?"
"I need a long-range business jet, fully fueled. I also want enough fuel reserves secured to support up to ten round trips between here and Antarctica."
Grayson didn’t respond immediately.
"And before you ask," Stan added, "I won’t need a pilot."
That earned him another, longer silence. When Grayson finally spoke, his voice remained calm, but there was unmistakable caution beneath the professionalism.
"Stan, if you don’t mind my asking..."
A slight pause.
"What exactly do you need this for?"
Stan considered giving a partial answer. Instead, he chose the truth.
"I need to go to Antarctica."
The silence that followed stretched several seconds.
When Grayson spoke again, something in his tone had changed.
"...Is this about the discovery beneath the glacier?"
Stan straightened slightly. "So you know about it."
"I’ve been briefed."
"By whom?"
"The families I maintain business relationships with."
Another pause.
"They’ve been mobilizing for the past two days. Several have already dispatched representatives south."
Stan’s eyes narrowed. "So it’s true."
Grayson gave a quiet, humorless chuckle. "I suppose it is."
He continued more carefully.
"If you’re asking me for an aircraft capable of reaching Antarctica, then you’re paying attention to the same signals they are."
A beat.
"I’ll admit, I wouldn’t have expected that from you before today."
"You’d be surprised."
"I suspect I would." Grayson shifted back into business. "Yes, I can arrange the aircraft."
Stan waited.

"There’s a Bombardier Global 8000 currently available through a broker I’ve worked with for years. It’s one of the few business jets with the range, performance, and operational flexibility suitable for what you’re describing."
He paused briefly. "It won’t be cheap."
"I’m not concerned about the price."
"The aircraft alone will cost several hundred million dollars."
"I expected that."
"Securing the fuel reserves you’ve requested, along with cold-weather support equipment and expedited delivery, will increase the total considerably."
"That’s fine."
Grayson was silent for a moment. "...I know money isn’t your concern."
Another pause.
"But even by your standards, this is going to be an expensive purchase."
"I have the balance."
"I don’t doubt it."
Grayson hesitated before continuing. "There is one complication."
"What is it?"
"Access."
Stan frowned, letting Grayson continue...
"Private aircraft can’t simply file a flight plan to Antarctica."

chapters.title: Chapter 309: Access Granted!
paragraphs: "Private aircraft can’t simply file a flight plan to Antarctica."
"They can’t?"
"No."

"The continent is governed by international treaty. Flights are heavily regulated. Without government authorization, an approved research mission, military coordination, or a recognized logistical operator, you won’t receive clearance."
He let that sink in. "If you’re planning to fly there legally, you’ll need institutional backing."
"And if I’m not?"
Another brief silence. "Then you’ll need a route that avoids needing permission."
Stan nodded to himself. "I understand."
"I’ll handle the aircraft."
"And I’ll handle everything else."
"Exactly." Grayson exhaled.
"Stan."
"Yes?"
"I don’t know what you’ve gotten yourself involved in."
His voice was quieter now. "But whatever this is, be careful."
"I will."
The call ended.
Stan set the phone down. Grayson had almost certainly become more suspicious of him.

The conversation had revealed far more than Stan normally allowed. A man casually authorizing the purchase of a private jet worth hundreds of millions of dollars, then announcing that he intended to fly to Antarctica alone, was not behaving like an ordinary corporate shareholder.
To someone as perceptive as Grayson, it would be obvious.
Stan was operating with access to information that wasn’t publicly available.
Grayson would draw his own conclusions. For now, that couldn’t be helped. His immediate problem remained unchanged.
"Access huh?"
He opened his laptop and began researching. An hour of careful reading painted a clear picture.
No private citizen could simply file a flight plan and fly into Antarctica.

The continent was governed under the Antarctic Treaty System, and access was tightly controlled. Scientific expeditions required authorization through national Antarctic programs. Tourist visits were restricted to approved operators following established routes. Even privately owned aircraft required extensive coordination, permits, and logistical support.
Flying there was less like visiting another country, and more like entering one of the most heavily managed environments on Earth.
Stan kept digging. Another hour of searching proved far more productive.
Buried beneath layers of aviation and logistics databases, he found references to a handful of highly specialized firms that quietly coordinated Antarctic operations for private clients.
Governments. Research foundations. Defense contractors. Energy companies. Ultra-high-net-worth individuals.
The industry was deliberately discreet, exceptionally expensive, and almost invisible to the public.
One company in particular caught his attention.
Grayson had mentioned it weeks earlier while discussing specialized international logistics.
Stan submitted an inquiry through its encrypted contact portal.
His secure phone rang less than thirty minutes later. He answered.
"This is Stan."
The woman on the other end spoke with calm, practiced professionalism.
"Mr. Stan. We received your request regarding a private Antarctic expedition."
"That’s right."
"May I ask which organization you represent?"
Stan considered the question. "No organization."
A brief pause. "...I’m sorry?"
"I’m traveling alone."
Silence. He could hear a keyboard clicking softly in the background.
She was updating his file.
When she spoke again, her tone remained courteous, though noticeably more careful.

"Mr. Stan, Antarctica is not a conventional travel destination. The majority of our clients are governments, scientific institutions, multinational corporations, or private organizations conducting authorized research."
"I understand."
"May I ask the purpose of your expedition?"
He had anticipated the question. "Independent research."
"What field?"
"Environmental anomalies."
The representative paused. "I see."
Her voice remained polite, but he could almost hear the skepticism.
"We would ordinarily require documentation supporting the project before proceeding. There are regulatory protocols we cannot simply bypass."
Stan suppressed a sigh. "So much for that."
He was already considering ending the call and searching for another avenue when she spoke again. "However..."
He stopped.
"There have been... unusual developments."
She chose the words carefully.
"Our company has received an exceptional number of confidential requests concerning Antarctica over the past forty-eight hours."
Stan said nothing.
"As a result, we’ve made certain accommodations for clients whose organizations require enhanced discretion."
Understanding dawned immediately.
The Spirit Pool.
The hidden families.
The wave of private aircraft heading south.

This company had spent the past two days fielding requests from exactly the sort of people Amelia had described, wealthy, anonymous clients arriving without public affiliations, demanding complete confidentiality.
The representative had reached the obvious conclusion.
She believed Stan was another member, or representative, of that same hidden circle.
He saw no reason to correct her.
"I require complete confidentiality."
The change in her tone was immediate.
"Naturally."
It wasn’t merely polite anymore.
It was respectful.
"Our clients’ identities are never disclosed."
She continued smoothly.
"We can arrange transportation using our own fleet, or, should your organization prefer, we can coordinate logistical support for a privately owned aircraft."
"I’m acquiring the aircraft separately."
"Very good."
Keys clicked softly again.
"In that case, we’ll provide operational support only."
She began listing the services.
"Flight planning."
"International clearances."
"Antarctic routing."
"Satellite tracking.
"Weather intelligence."
"Ground coordination."
"Emergency response."
"Insurance."
She paused. "Given the current level of demand, I estimate the operational support package will cost between seven and ten million dollars, exclusive of aircraft acquisition."
"That’s acceptable."
"I thought it might be."
There was the faintest hint of a smile in her voice.
"May I record that your organization wishes to remain anonymous throughout the operation?"
"Yes."
"Understood."
A few more keystrokes.
"Everything will be prepared immediately. You’ll receive an encrypted itinerary as soon as your aircraft details are finalized."
"Thank you."
"It was a pleasure speaking with you, Mr. Stan."
The call ended. Stan lowered the phone.
He leaned back in his chair and let out a quiet breath.
"...That went considerably better than I expected."
For the first time since the system had issued its mission, getting to Antarctica no longer seemed like the difficult part.
Getting there first, that was going to be the real challenge.
A system notification appeared.
[Side Mission Triggered.]
[Objective: Travel to Antarctica.]
[Reward: Profession Skill, Chef (Master).]
Stan glanced at the message and smiled faintly. "Perfect."
A useful skill upgrade attached to something he was already going to do. He had no intention of complaining.
He closed the laptop and stood from the dining table.

He did not know that, in the same moment he declined to name any organizational affiliation while casually committing hundreds of millions of dollars to an Antarctic expedition, the logistics firm handling his inquiry had quietly assigned him a classification.
Not a formal one. An internal one. A typical high-net-worth actor. Unidentified backing. Likely affiliated with non-publicized legacy capital group.
It was speculative. But in their line of work, speculation was often the first stage of caution.

Within the hour, that classification would be passed, informally, discreetly, to a small network of private polar logistics operators who shared intelligence out of necessity in an industry built on silence and discretion.
Within four hours, variations of the same note would begin circulating through secure channels in at least two national intelligence agencies.
Not because Stan had done anything illegal.
But because a single wealthy individual, operating without institutional cover, was now independently organizing Antarctic access at a scale usually reserved for states and multinational consortiums.
And more importantly, no one could identify who was backing him.
In intelligence terms, that was worse than transparency.
It was ambiguity with capital. And ambiguity with capital was almost always treated as a signal of hidden power.
Stan, entirely unaware of any of this, left his apartment and headed for the gym.
A light warm-up. A routine session.
Something normal before a very abnormal trip.
The next few days, he suspected, were going to be interesting.
He was right. Just not in the way he thought.

[Objective: Travel to Antarctica.]
[Reward: Profession Skill, Chef (Master).]
Stan glanced at the message and smiled faintly.
"Perfect."
A useful skill upgrade attached to something he was already going to do.
He had no intention of complaining.
He closed the laptop and stood from the dining table.

He did not know that, in the same moment he declined to name any organizational affiliation while casually committing hundreds of millions of dollars to an Antarctic expedition, the logistics firm handling his inquiry had quietly assigned him a classification.
Not a formal one.
An internal one.
A typical high-net-worth actor.
Unidentified backing.
Likely affiliated with non-publicized legacy capital group.
It was speculative.
But in their line of work, speculation was often the first stage of caution.

Within the hour, that classification would be passed, informally, discreetly, to a small network of private polar logistics operators who shared intelligence out of necessity in an industry built on silence and discretion.
Within four hours, variations of the same note would begin circulating through secure channels in at least two national intelligence agencies.
Not because Stan had done anything illegal.
But because a single wealthy individual, operating without institutional cover, was now independently organizing Antarctic access at a scale usually reserved for states and multinational consortiums.
And more importantly, no one could identify who was backing him.
In intelligence terms, that was worse than transparency.
It was ambiguity with capital.
And ambiguity with capital was almost always treated as a signal of hidden power.
Stan, entirely unaware of any of this, left his apartment and headed for the gym.
A light warm-up.
A routine session.
Something normal before a very abnormal trip.
The next few days, he suspected, were going to be interesting.
He was right.
Just not in the way he thought.

chapters.title: Chapter 310: Goodbyes
paragraphs: Grayson’s message arrived just as Stan was finishing some routine work.
[Grayson: I’ve finished negotiating with the supplier.]
Stan pulled out his phone and replied.
[Stan: The aircraft?]
[Grayson: One of the most capable long-range private jets currently available. They’ve also agreed to every modification you requested. Full package attached below.]
The next message contained a detailed itemized list. Stan opened the attachment and scrolled through it.

From polar operations package, extreme cold-weather reinforcement of the private jet and advanced de-icing systems, emergency survival equipment, long-range communications suite, satellite navigation package, Multiple spare engines to large reserve of Jet A-1 fuel.

Stan nodded upon reading through it, it was very reasonable, after all he was getting a custom jet, not just any custom jet but on customed for Antarctica level of coldness, which can go to as low as -89°C which is really crazy...
Anyways, he look and saw Grayson reply...
[Grayson: The total comes to just under five hundred million U.S. dollars. Payment can be made whenever it suits your schedule.]
Stan didn’t hesitate.
[Stan: I’ll transfer the funds now.]
A moment later, another message appeared.
[Grayson: ... Alright.]
After Stan did the transfer Grayson sent him another message a few minutes later;
[The aircraft is fueled, fully prepared, and waiting at the company’s private airfield. It can depart within the hour as soon as you arrive.]
[Stan: Good.]
He slipped the phone back into his pocket. There wasn’t much time.

The system had given him a seven-day window, but he doubted he had that long in practice. The old families Amelia’s intelligence had identified were already mobilizing. Every hour they gained was another hour he’d have to claw back.
Every minute counted.
Before leaving Inksea, Stan made a series of calls.
He sat at his dining table, mentally arranged them in order of emotional proximity, and worked through them one by one.
Sophie first. She answered on the second ring, her voice carrying the quiet warmth she reserved for him alone.
"Stan?"
"Sophie. I’m going away for a while. Business."
"...Business."
"Something like that."
A brief silence followed.
Sophie possessed an almost uncanny instinct for recognizing the boundaries he wouldn’t cross. Something like that told her there were answers he wasn’t prepared to give.
She didn’t press.
"How long?"
"I’m not sure. A few days at least. Maybe a week and a half."
"Where are you going?"
"Somewhere with unreliable signal."
"Stan."
"Yes?"
"Is it safe?"
"Yes."
"Are you telling me the truth?"
"I am."
Another pause.
When she spoke again, her voice was softer.
"Just come back safely."
"I will."
"I mean it." She exhaled quietly. "I have a bad feeling about this, and I don’t know why. Just... come back."
"Sophie."
"Yes?"
"I’ll come back."
She let out a small, unsteady breath. "Okay."
"I’ll call you the moment I have signal again."
"You’d better."
The call ended.
Sarah next.
She answered almost immediately, her cheerful voice brightening the line.
"Stan, hi."
"Sarah. Just a quick call. I’ll be away for about a week, maybe a little longer. Reception’s probably going to be poor."
"Oh."
A brief pause as she adjusted.
"Where are you headed?"
"Work."
"Are you okay?"
"I’m fine.
"You’d tell me if you weren’t?"
"I would."
She was quiet for a moment.
"I’ll miss you, Stan."
"I’ll miss you too, Sarah."
Another pause.
"I’ll bring you something back."
"You don’t have to."
"I know."
His voice softened.
"I want to."
She smiled, and he could hear it.
"Then... something small. Nothing extravagant."
"Something small and thoughtful. Got it."
Another beat passed before she spoke again, more quietly this time.
"Come back to me."
"I will."
The line went silent.
He then called Maya who answered with the playful tone that had become her default with him since their dinner together.
"Business investor calling to check on his investment?"
"Business investor calling to say he’ll be off-grid for a while."
"Off-grid?" Her voice sharpened ever so slightly. "Off-grid where?"
"Overseas. Somewhere with unreliable reception. About a week, maybe a little longer."
"Stan."
"Yes?"
"Is this film opportunity off-grid, or someone’s trying to kill you off-grid?"
He almost laughed. "Neither. Just private business."
"That’s not remotely reassuring."
"It isn’t meant to be ominous. It’s just a trip."
"Straightforward trips don’t usually come with a warning that you’ll disappear off the grid."
"You’re too perceptive for your own good."
"I know." She sighed. "I’m still going to worry."
"Then try not to."
"That’s not how worrying works."
He smiled despite himself.
"Maya."
"Yes?"
"I’ll be back. And when I am, I’ll tell you the whole story."
"The whole story?"
"As much of it as I can."
She huffed softly. "That’s not quite the same thing."
"It’s the best I can offer right now."
A brief silence settled between them.
"Come back safe, Stan Harrison."
"I will."
The call ended.
Mia fourth.

She answered almost breathlessly, the way she always did now, the eager inhale of someone who had spent nine years believing he’d disappeared from her life, and who still hadn’t quite grown used to seeing his name appear on her phone.
"Stan!"
"Mia."
"Where are you? Are you coming over?"
"Not this week. I’m calling because I’ll be away for a little while."
"...Away?"
"Traveling somewhere remote. Reception’s going to be unreliable."
Her excitement faded at once.
"How long?"
"About a week. Ten days at the most."
There was a tiny tremor in her voice when she spoke again.
"Stan... you’re coming back, right?"
"I’m coming back."
"You promise?"
"I promise.
"You really mean it?"
"I do."
He paused before adding gently,
"This isn’t nine years. It’s one week."
A quiet laugh escaped her, fragile despite itself.
"I’ll still miss you."
"I know."
"Mom’s going to ask if you called."
"I’ll message her as soon as I’m back."
"...Okay."
"Mia."
"Yeah?"
"I’ll see you soon."
"I’ll hold you to that."
Then he called Xenia. She answered in the polished, professional voice she used at Star Entertainment.
"Sir Stan."
"Xenia. Just a quick heads-up. I’ll be off-grid for about a week, possibly a little longer."
"Understood."
"If anything urgent comes up, Vivian has interim authority to handle escalations. She already knows the chain of command, but I wanted you informed."
"Understood, Sir Stan. Anything else?"
"Nothing operational."
He paused.
"And... thank you. You’ve kept everything running smoothly."
Her voice softened almost imperceptibly.
"It’s my pleasure, Sir Stan."
Another brief pause.
"Please return safely."
"I intend to."
Amelia after that. He gave her Vivian’s contact incase she got results from Vanguard about the Fake Streak they were investigating
Vivian was next. The conversation was brief and entirely professional.

He confirmed that she would hold interim authority over Star Entertainment’s escalation chain during his absence, reminded her that Amelia’s operation involving the Streak impersonator would continue as planned, and assured her that the arrangements concerning her brother remained in place if she needed anything while he was away.
Vivian thanked him formally and wished him a safe journey before ending the call.
Then finally was his sister, She answered on the third ring, surprise quickly giving way to concern, the instinctive shift she always had whenever her younger brother called unexpectedly.
"Stan?"
"Sis."
"You never call at this hour. What’s wrong?"
She always knew. "I’m traveling for a week or so. Maybe ten days. Reception will be spotty."
The silence that followed was longer than any he’d encountered during the other calls.
"...Where are you going?"
"It’s business."
"Stan."
"Sis."
"You’re not going to tell me where."
"No."
"Why?"
He drew a slow breath. "Because I don’t want you worrying."
"Stan."
Her voice changed.
It was no longer the casual concern of an older sister. It was the voice of a sister who had stepped into the role of parent when theirs disappeared.
The voice that had argued with landlords, stretched every dollar, and carried them both through years that should have broken them.
Just as he thought she was about to scold him or something, her voice softened slightly..
"You’re a Grown up now Stan, you can take care of yourself and stay safe... I don’t want you to dissapear like mum and dad..."
A faint smile tugged at his lips. "Fair."
"I love you."
"I love you too, sis."
"Come home."
"I will."
The call ended. Stan lowered the phone but didn’t move.
For a long moment, he simply sat there, staring at the blank screen in his hand.
Then he stood.

He walked into his bedroom and packed a small backpack with a change of clothes, and a few essentials, everything important he might need, water, drinks, they were all put to his inventory and then he left...
When he left the apartment, he hailed a taxi. He didn’t have someone to drive his car back if he used that, so a taxi was more convenient...
