chapters.title: Chapter 311: Departure
paragraphs: Hours later, Stan arrived at the company’s private aviation facility on the outskirts of the city.

As he stepped out of the vehicle, three suited executives stood waiting at the entrance to the private terminal. Their posture was crisp, their expressions respectful, their demeanor carefully restrained, the polished professionalism of a company dealing with a discreet, high-value client determined to prove it understood exactly who he was.
The man at the front, a tall, silver-haired executive in his sixties whose effortless composure spoke of decades negotiating aircraft sales at the highest level, stepped forward and extended a hand.
"Mr. Stan. Welcome. I’m Klaus Werner, Senior Director of Client Services. We’ve completed every modification you requested. If you’ll follow us, we’d be pleased to walk you through the aircraft."
Stan shook his hand.
"Thank you."

The executives escorted him across the vast private hangar. Cold industrial lights shone from the ceiling, reflecting off the spotless concrete floor. The air carried the faint scent of aviation fuel mixed with fresh hangar wax.
Then the aircraft came into view.
Stan slowed to a stop.

The sleek white business jet rested beneath the lights like a masterpiece of modern engineering. Its polished fuselage reflected the overhead illumination in long, shimmering bands. Gracefully swept wings extended from either side, while every visible surface, the engine nacelles, landing gear, fuselage panels, and T-tail, displayed the quiet precision expected of a top-tier long-range business jet prepared with exceptional care.
Werner smiled with understated pride.

"This aircraft has been specially configured for sustained polar operations, Mr. Stan. The airframe has been reinforced to withstand prolonged exposure to extreme cold. The cabin features enhanced thermal insulation, and we’ve upgraded the anti-icing systems across every critical surface. There are three redundant emergency locator beacons, satellite communications with full polar coverage, a portable emergency shelter, expanded medical supplies, comprehensive cold-weather survival equipment, and freeze-resistant rations sufficient for two weeks in the event of an emergency landing."
He gestured toward the aircraft.
"Every modification has been installed, secured, and verified. Our polar operations team has tested every system twice. The aircraft is ready for departure the moment you authorize it."
Stan walked slowly along the length of the fuselage, his gaze lingering over every detail.
The engine intakes, the landing gear, the panel seams, the de-icing systems lining the wing’s leading edges, the auxiliary power unit housed beneath the tail, the fuel dump vents.
With every glance, the system’s newly acquired Master Pilot certification quietly supplied information.
He quickly confirmed that the engine condition, hydraulic pressure, aurframe integrity were all okay.
Then he checked to confirm that the main and auxiliary tanks had been loaded to standard capacity.
Every sweep of his eyes generated a precise real-time assessment, one that, only 24 hours ago, he would have had neither the knowledge nor the experience to make. Now it felt effortless.
As though he had spent decades performing pre-flight inspections.
After a final look, he gave a small nod. "It’ll do."
Werner and the other executives released nearly imperceptible sighs of relief.

Stan noticed immediately, suppressing a flicker of amusement. They had clearly expected that a client of his apparent stature might discover some flaw or demand further changes. His simple approval had lifted an invisible weight from their shoulders.
"Is the primary fuel tank full?"
"Completely fueled, Mr. Stan," Werner replied. "Both main tanks and the auxiliary."
"And the reserve fuel I ordered?"
Werner’s smile widened just enough to betray his satisfaction.
"Everything you specified has been loaded."
He gestured toward the aircraft’s cargo section.
"If you’ll follow me."
They led him across the hangar to a secured storage facility.
Stan stopped as he took in what awaited him.

Hundreds of industrial fuel containers stood in neat, disciplined rows, each roughly the size of a compact car. Every container bore the aviation supplier’s markings and was filled with premium Jet A-1 fuel. Together, they stretched across the concrete floor in a perfectly organized grid, a layout that spoke of ground crews with near-military precision.
Werner spread a hand toward them.

"Approximately five hundred thousand liters of premium Jet A-1 fuel," he said with quiet satisfaction. "Exactly as requested. Enough to support the ten round trips to Antarctica you outlined, with a generous operational reserve for diversions or extended holding."
Stan gave a single nod.
"Good."
He walked toward the nearest row of containers.
The logistics coordinator standing nearby, a middle-aged employee with a clipboard tucked beneath one arm, stepped politely aside, assuming the client simply wanted to inspect the shipment.
Stan stopped.
One hand rested casually at his side.
His mind reached into the System.
The inventory activated without a sound.
The nearest container vanished.
A heartbeat later, another disappeared.
Then another.
And another.
The pace quickened.
There was no flash of light, no distortion of space, no audible cue. The containers simply ceased to exist where they stood, disappearing one after another at the speed of Stan’s thoughts.
Row after row dissolved into his spatial inventory.
Forty seconds later, it was over.
Five hundred thousand liters of aviation fuel now rested inside his personal storage.
The warehouse was empty.
Only the concrete pads remained, marking where the containers had stood moments earlier.
The logistics coordinator happened to glance back.
He froze.
His eyes swept across the vacant floor.
Then to Stan.
Then back to the empty pads.
His mouth parted.
Stan turned, wearing the calm, mildly distracted expression of someone interrupted during an entirely ordinary inspection.
"Yes?"
"The fuel containers..."
"Yes?"
"...You don’t need them loaded onto the aircraft?"
"No."
The coordinator blinked.
"I’ll have someone collect them later."
A pause.
"...The empty containers?"
"Correct."
The coordinator looked once more at the bare concrete.
There were no containers.
There had unquestionably been containers less than a minute ago.
His mind attempted to reconcile the undeniable evidence before him with every law of physics it had ever accepted.
It failed.
Then professionalism prevailed.
He was a logistics coordinator serving wealthy private clients, not an investigator assigned to question impossible events.
He gave a slow nod.
"Very well, sir."
Without another word, he returned to his clipboard and resumed making notes.
Stan walked toward the far side of the storage area and took out his phone.
He dialed Grayson.
The call was answered on the second ring.
"Young Master."

"Grayson. I’ve emptied the fuel containers into the aircraft’s primary storage system. The containers themselves are no longer needed. I’d like you to send a small team to collect them from the airfield. Charge any associated costs to my personal accounts."
There was a brief silence.
"...Collect the containers.
"Yes."
"Empty?"
"Empty."
Another pause.
"But, Sir Stan, won’t you need the containers to transport the fuel during the mission?"
"No."
A beat passed.
"I have an alternative storage solution."
Grayson remained silent for a moment before replying in the measured tone of a man who had long since learned that his employer occasionally made requests best accepted without further inquiry.
"...Understood. I’ll dispatch a team immediately."
"Thank you."
"Anything else, Sir Stan?"
"Nothing further."
"Safe travels."
"Thank you, Grayson."
The call ended.
To the logistics coordinator, and to anyone else who might ask, the explanation would be perfectly mundane.

Stan’s private team would arrive shortly, collect the now-empty fuel containers, and transport them off-site for whatever purpose their employer required. The paperwork would reflect nothing more than an unusually wealthy client managing his own logistics.
No one would suspect anything extraordinary.
After all, ordinary people knew nothing of spatial inventories or supernatural storage.
When presented with an impossible event, most people instinctively reached for the most ordinary explanation available.
Stan preferred it that way.
Satisfied, he slipped his phone back into his pocket and headed toward the waiting aircraft.
Werner was waiting beside the aircraft, a tablet in hand.
"Mr. Stan. Just one final step."
He held out the device.

"Your flight registration has been completed. The aircraft’s identification signature and transponder code have been filed with the relevant aviation authorities under a private commercial designation. Your route to the subcontinental staging area has been acknowledged. As long as your transponder remains active and you file your onward Antarctic flight plan through the discreet channel we discussed, your aircraft will be recognized as authorized commercial traffic while transiting controlled airspace."
Stan accepted the tablet and reviewed the digital authorization package.
Satisfied, he pressed his thumb against the biometric confirmation panel. The display flashed green.
[Registration Accepted. Aircraft Cleared for Departure.]
Werner inclined his head. "Have a productive expedition, Mr. Stan. We’ll be here when you return."
"Thank you, Werner."
The two men shook hands one last time.
Stan turned and made his way toward the aircraft’s boarding stairs.
As he climbed, he glanced back once.
Werner and his colleagues still stood at the edge of the hangar, watching him depart.
Their expressions remained impeccably professional, yet beneath that polished composure lingered unmistakable astonishment.

In the span of a single day, they had overseen a cash purchase worth half a billion dollars, supervised a fully customized polar retrofit completed on an impossible timetable, and served a solitary client with no visible corporate, governmental, or military affiliation. They were half in shock.
Anyways, Stan uncaring for what they were thinking reached the top of the stairs, ducked into the cabin, and pulled the door shut behind him.
With that, the Antarctic expedition had officially begun.
End Of Volume 1...
Thanks for following me on this journey

Their posture was crisp, their expressions respectful, their demeanor carefully restrained, the polished professionalism of a company dealing with a discreet, high-value client determined to prove it understood exactly who he was.
The man at the front, a tall, silver-haired executive in his sixties whose effortless composure spoke of decades negotiating aircraft sales at the highest level, stepped forward and extended a hand.
"Mr.
Stan.
Welcome.
I’m Klaus Werner, Senior Director of Client Services.
We’ve completed every modification you requested.
If you’ll follow us, we’d be pleased to walk you through the aircraft."
Stan shook his hand.
"Thank you."
The executives escorted him across the vast private hangar.
Cold industrial lights shone from the ceiling, reflecting off the spotless concrete floor.
The air carried the faint scent of aviation fuel mixed with fresh hangar wax.
Then the aircraft came into view.
Stan slowed to a stop.
The sleek white business jet rested beneath the lights like a masterpiece of modern engineering.
Its polished fuselage reflected the overhead illumination in long, shimmering bands.

Gracefully swept wings extended from either side, while every visible surface, the engine nacelles, landing gear, fuselage panels, and T-tail, displayed the quiet precision expected of a top-tier long-range business jet prepared with exceptional care.
Werner smiled with understated pride.
"This aircraft has been specially configured for sustained polar operations, Mr.
Stan.
The airframe has been reinforced to withstand prolonged exposure to extreme cold.
The cabin features enhanced thermal insulation, and we’ve upgraded the anti-icing systems across every critical surface.

There are three redundant emergency locator beacons, satellite communications with full polar coverage, a portable emergency shelter, expanded medical supplies, comprehensive cold-weather survival equipment, and freeze-resistant rations sufficient for two weeks in the event of an emergency landing."
He gestured toward the aircraft.
"Every modification has been installed, secured, and verified.
Our polar operations team has tested every system twice.
The aircraft is ready for departure the moment you authorize it."
Stan walked slowly along the length of the fuselage, his gaze lingering over every detail.
The engine intakes, the landing gear, the panel seams, the de-icing systems lining the wing’s leading edges, the auxiliary power unit housed beneath the tail, the fuel dump vents.
With every glance, the system’s newly acquired Master Pilot certification quietly supplied information.
He quickly confirmed that the engine condition, hydraulic pressure, aurframe integrity were all okay.
Then he checked to confirm that the main and auxiliary tanks had been loaded to standard capacity.
Every sweep of his eyes generated a precise real-time assessment, one that, only 24 hours ago, he would have had neither the knowledge nor the experience to make.
Now it felt effortless.
As though he had spent decades performing pre-flight inspections.
After a final look, he gave a small nod.
"It’ll do."
Werner and the other executives released nearly imperceptible sighs of relief.
Stan noticed immediately, suppressing a flicker of amusement.
They had clearly expected that a client of his apparent stature might discover some flaw or demand further changes.
His simple approval had lifted an invisible weight from their shoulders.
"Is the primary fuel tank full?"
"Completely fueled, Mr.
Stan," Werner replied.
"Both main tanks and the auxiliary."
"And the reserve fuel I ordered?"
Werner’s smile widened just enough to betray his satisfaction.
"Everything you specified has been loaded."
He gestured toward the aircraft’s cargo section.
"If you’ll follow me."
They led him across the hangar to a secured storage facility.
Stan stopped as he took in what awaited him.
Hundreds of industrial fuel containers stood in neat, disciplined rows, each roughly the size of a compact car.
Every container bore the aviation supplier’s markings and was filled with premium Jet A-1 fuel.
Together, they stretched across the concrete floor in a perfectly organized grid, a layout that spoke of ground crews with near-military precision.
Werner spread a hand toward them.
"Approximately five hundred thousand liters of premium Jet A-1 fuel," he said with quiet satisfaction.
"Exactly as requested.
Enough to support the ten round trips to Antarctica you outlined, with a generous operational reserve for diversions or extended holding."
Stan gave a single nod.
"Good."
He walked toward the nearest row of containers.
The logistics coordinator standing nearby, a middle-aged employee with a clipboard tucked beneath one arm, stepped politely aside, assuming the client simply wanted to inspect the shipment.
Stan stopped.
One hand rested casually at his side.
His mind reached into the System.
The inventory activated without a sound.
The nearest container vanished.
A heartbeat later, another disappeared.
Then another.
And another.
The pace quickened.
There was no flash of light, no distortion of space, no audible cue.
The containers simply ceased to exist where they stood, disappearing one after another at the speed of Stan’s thoughts.
Row after row dissolved into his spatial inventory.
Forty seconds later, it was over.
Five hundred thousand liters of aviation fuel now rested inside his personal storage.
The warehouse was empty.
Only the concrete pads remained, marking where the containers had stood moments earlier.
The logistics coordinator happened to glance back.
He froze.
His eyes swept across the vacant floor.
Then to Stan.
Then back to the empty pads.
His mouth parted.
Stan turned, wearing the calm, mildly distracted expression of someone interrupted during an entirely ordinary inspection.
"Yes?"
"The fuel containers..."
"Yes?"
"...You don’t need them loaded onto the aircraft?"
"No."
The coordinator blinked.
"I’ll have someone collect them later."
A pause.
"...The empty containers?"
"Correct."
The coordinator looked once more at the bare concrete.
There were no containers.
There had unquestionably been containers less than a minute ago.
His mind attempted to reconcile the undeniable evidence before him with every law of physics it had ever accepted.
It failed.
Then professionalism prevailed.
He was a logistics coordinator serving wealthy private clients, not an investigator assigned to question impossible events.
He gave a slow nod.
"Very well, sir."
Without another word, he returned to his clipboard and resumed making notes.
Stan walked toward the far side of the storage area and took out his phone.
He dialed Grayson.
The call was answered on the second ring.
"Young Master."
"Grayson.
I’ve emptied the fuel containers into the aircraft’s primary storage system.
The containers themselves are no longer needed.
I’d like you to send a small team to collect them from the airfield.
Charge any associated costs to my personal accounts."
There was a brief silence.
"...Collect the containers.
"Yes."
"Empty?"
"Empty."
Another pause.
"But, Sir Stan, won’t you need the containers to transport the fuel during the mission?"
"No."
A beat passed.
"I have an alternative storage solution."
Grayson remained silent for a moment before replying in the measured tone of a man who had long since learned that his employer occasionally made requests best accepted without further inquiry.
"...Understood.
I’ll dispatch a team immediately."
"Thank you."
"Anything else, Sir Stan?"
"Nothing further."
"Safe travels."
"Thank you, Grayson."
The call ended.
To the logistics coordinator, and to anyone else who might ask, the explanation would be perfectly mundane.
Stan’s private team would arrive shortly, collect the now-empty fuel containers, and transport them off-site for whatever purpose their employer required.
The paperwork would reflect nothing more than an unusually wealthy client managing his own logistics.
No one would suspect anything extraordinary.
After all, ordinary people knew nothing of spatial inventories or supernatural storage.
When presented with an impossible event, most people instinctively reached for the most ordinary explanation available.
Stan preferred it that way.
Satisfied, he slipped his phone back into his pocket and headed toward the waiting aircraft.
Werner was waiting beside the aircraft, a tablet in hand.
"Mr.
Stan.
Just one final step."
He held out the device.
"Your flight registration has been completed.
The aircraft’s identification signature and transponder code have been filed with the relevant aviation authorities under a private commercial designation.
Your route to the subcontinental staging area has been acknowledged.

As long as your transponder remains active and you file your onward Antarctic flight plan through the discreet channel we discussed, your aircraft will be recognized as authorized commercial traffic while transiting controlled airspace."
Stan accepted the tablet and reviewed the digital authorization package.
Satisfied, he pressed his thumb against the biometric confirmation panel.
The display flashed green.
[Registration Accepted.
Aircraft Cleared for Departure.]
Werner inclined his head.
"Have a productive expedition, Mr.
Stan.
We’ll be here when you return."
"Thank you, Werner."
The two men shook hands one last time.
Stan turned and made his way toward the aircraft’s boarding stairs.
As he climbed, he glanced back once.
Werner and his colleagues still stood at the edge of the hangar, watching him depart.
Their expressions remained impeccably professional, yet beneath that polished composure lingered unmistakable astonishment.

In the span of a single day, they had overseen a cash purchase worth half a billion dollars, supervised a fully customized polar retrofit completed on an impossible timetable, and served a solitary client with no visible corporate, governmental, or military affiliation.
They were half in shock.
Anyways, Stan uncaring for what they were thinking reached the top of the stairs, ducked into the cabin, and pulled the door shut behind him.
With that, the Antarctic expedition had officially begun.
End Of Volume 1...
Thanks for following me on this journey

chapters.title: Chapter 312: Leap Of Faith
paragraphs: The takeoff was flawless.

The polar-modified Bombardier lifted smoothly from the private airfield’s runway, climbing with the effortless confidence of a top-tier long-range business jet flown by a fully rated pilot, a qualification the system had quietly granted Stan barely twelve hours earlier.
The initial climb was uneventful.

Air Traffic Control cleared him through Inksea’s regional airspace without incident before handing him off to the transoceanic control network as the aircraft leveled off at its cruising altitude of forty-one thousand feet.
Stan engaged the autopilot, confirmed the polar flight plan, gave the instruments one last sweep, and let the aircraft do exactly what it had been engineered to do.
The next ten hours passed in the slow, almost hypnotic rhythm unique to long-haul, high-altitude flight.

Beyond the cockpit windows, the sky transformed by degrees. The warm golden hues of Inksea’s morning gradually faded into the pale, crystalline blue of the upper atmosphere before deepening into the rich sapphire that marked the approach to the far southern latitudes.

Far below, the ocean slipped endlessly beneath him at eight hundred and fifty kilometers per hour. Tropical waters gave way to temperate seas, their brilliant blues slowly surrendering to colder shades of steel-gray as the latitude increased.
Somewhere over the vast Pacific, the aircraft crossed the equator.
Hours later, as it continued south, daylight itself began to change. The familiar rhythm of the sun faded, replaced by the strange, lingering twilight that belonged only to the polar regions.
Stan sat quietly in the cockpit, watching the world drift beneath him.
His thoughts remained fixed on the Spirit Pool.
By now, the great families were almost certainly ahead of him.

According to Amelia’s intelligence briefing, several private jets had filed flight plans toward Antarctic staging airports over the previous forty-eight hours. Some would already have landed. Others would already have deployed their teams onto the ice.
Which meant he couldn’t afford the conventional approach.

Ordinarily, anyone traveling to Antarctica would land at one of the continent’s handful of designated runways, all operated by scientific programs or national research organizations. From there came clearance procedures, logistical coordination, weather windows, and carefully planned transport across the ice.
That process took days.
Possibly more than a week.
Stan didn’t have that kind of time.

If he intended to reach the Spirit Pool before everyone else, there was only one option left, one that no airfield operator, no one in Grayson’s office, none of Amelia’s Vanguard personnel, and certainly no controller monitoring Antarctic airspace would ever imagine a client like him attempting.
He wasn’t going to land.
He was going to fly directly over the Spirit Pool.
Then, at the precise moment... He was going to abandon the aircraft in midair. Well he was technically not going to abandon the air craft since he had a plan that should work 100 percent?
The system’s navigation arrow remained fixed in the corner of Stan’s vision as the Bombardier crossed the sixtieth parallel.

The Spirit Pool glowed as a distinct point of light roughly eleven hundred kilometers into the Antarctic interior, far beyond the continent’s handful of runways, beyond every research station, and deep inside a region no permit-holding civilian aircraft had any legitimate reason to approach.
Before leaving controlled airspace, he filed a false onward heading with the last regional controller capable of tracking him.
Thirty minutes later, once he was well beyond meaningful radar coverage, he quietly deviated from it.
Then he began his descent.

At forty thousand feet, Antarctica stretched beneath him as an endless expanse of blinding white. The vast ice sheet was broken only by the faint shadows of buried mountain ridges and thin veins of blue where ancient pressure fractures scarred the glacier.
Outside, the air was lethally cold.
At this altitude, exposed flesh would freeze in seconds, while the atmosphere was so thin that the Bombardier’s pressurization system worked constantly to keep the cabin habitable.
He descended further.
Twenty thousand feet!
Ten thousand!
Five thousand!

The polar-modified aircraft handled beautifully. The knowledge the system had implanted into his mind processed every stream of telemetry with calm, practiced efficiency, making each correction instinctive. The instruments remained steady. The de-icing system, active since entering Antarctic airspace, kept the wings and control surfaces free of ice.
Two thousand feet. Individual ridges and wind-carved drifts became visible.
One thousand feet. The wind indicators climbed sharply.

Katabatic winds swept across the Antarctic plateau with brutal unpredictability, buffeting the aircraft from multiple directions. Stan’s hands remained light on the controls, correcting each disturbance before it could develop into anything more.
Five hundred feet. He was directly above the Spirit Pool.
The pool itself remained invisible, buried beneath layers of ancient glacial ice. From above, there was nothing to distinguish it from the endless frozen wilderness.
Only the system’s arrow, perfectly centered in his vision, confirmed he had reached his destination.
He eased the throttles back.
The Bombardier began to slow. Still descending. Three hundred feet.
He was now well below the altitude from which any pilot would even consider attempting a landing.
There was no runway. No prepared ice strip.
Nothing but a landscape of jagged sastrugi, hidden crevasses, and hardened pressure ridges capable of ripping apart an aircraft the instant its landing gear touched down.
He had never intended to land. Two hundred feet. He pulled the throttles fully to idle. The aircraft began to sink faster. One hundred and fifty feet.
The stall warning chimed.

Its calm electronic tone quickly became more insistent as the aircraft bled below safe flying speed. Lift deteriorated. The Bombardier’s systems politely, but urgently, informed him that the aircraft was about to fall from the sky.
One hundred feet.
Stan rose from the pilot’s seat. He crossed the cabin in three unhurried strides.

His backpack was already secured. The insulated polar survival suit provided by the airfield covered him from head to toe, designed to keep a human alive in temperatures that would otherwise kill within minutes. He didn’t need it but he weared in anyways...
He reached the aft passenger door.
Fifty feet.
The aircraft slipped into a shallow but accelerating descent. One wing dipped lower than the other as the stalled airflow began robbing the controls of authority.
Stan wrapped his hand around the door lever.
Thirty feet. He pulled.
The Antarctic wind slammed into the cabin like a battering ram.
Pressurized air exploded outward in a deafening roar, instantly followed by the savage howl of sub-zero polar air. Every warning system erupted at once.
Cockpit alarms screamed. The stall warning became one continuous shriek. The aircraft rolled harder.
Stan stepped into the open doorway.
The frozen surface rushed toward him with terrifying speed, close enough for every instinct in his body to recognize a simple, undeniable truth.
No ordinary human could survive this. But he was no longer ordinary. Taking one slow, steady breath... Stan jumped.
The wind seized him the instant he cleared the doorway. He fell at rapid speed...

Above him, the Bombardier continued along the trajectory of its final descent. Its right wing dropped farther, the nose pitched lower, and thirty tons of polar-modified engineering hurtled toward an impact only seconds away.
Stan spread his arms just enough to stabilize himself.

The bitter Antarctic wind clawed at his insulated gear. Frigid air whipped past his face, forcing his eyes into a narrow squint, yet his mind remained perfectly calm. Under the system’s enhancements, every sensation seemed sharper, every calculation clearer, every passing second stretched into effortless clarity.
He raised one hand toward the aircraft. Then willed it into his inventory.
The Bombardier vanished.
One moment, the half-billion-dollar jet was there, committed to its fatal descent.
The next... The sky above him was empty.
The thunder of the engines ceased as though someone had flipped a switch.
The relentless stall warning disappeared with it.
Only the endless roar of the Antarctic wind remained.
Stan watched the empty sky for a heartbeat before a faint smile tugged at the corner of his mouth.
’Not bad.’

chapters.title: Chapter 313: Visitors from the Old World
paragraphs: Stan watched the empty sky for a heartbeat before a faint smile tugged at the corner of his mouth.
’Not bad.’

He had perhaps six seconds before impact. The bone-tempering that had rewritten his skeleton the previous day had, by his best estimate, made him roughly five times more physically durable than an ordinary human.

The jade purity elixir had reinforced everything else. The qi circulating through his body now added an additional layer of shock absorption that the elixir had, in some way he did not yet fully understand, activated in his muscles.
He was as prepared for a high-altitude landing as anyone in the modern world could be with a parachute.

But he had also never actually tested this. He was, in the most literal sense, about to find out whether his current physiological baseline could survive a fall from what had to be at least two hundred feet.
’With my tempered bones and the elixir’s reinforcement, I should be able to survive this... Right?’ He thought as he braced.

He shifted his body posture in the fall the way his newly-integrated martial arts mastery told him to, legs slightly bent, spine aligned, weight distributed to absorb the impact through the largest possible surface area.
His combat training, decades of knowledge installed into his mind hours earlier, took over the landing preparation with the calm, unhurried efficiency of a discipline he had somehow always known.
Three seconds to impact.
He picked his landing spot, a patch of relatively level snow, wind-packed and dense, roughly forty meters from the surface point above the Spirit Pool.
’Two seconds.’ He centered himself.
’One second!’
He hit the ice with full force!
The impact was enormous!

His feet drove into the compressed snow with the force of a heavy truck at highway speed. His knees flexed, absorbing the initial shock, and his body continued downward into the powder as the momentum carried through his frame.

The snow beneath him crumpled and compacted around his boots. The impact rippled outward through his skeleton in a wave of pressure that he felt, clearly, distinctly, the specific sensation of his bones registering the load and holding it, but did not break under.
His knees compressed to nearly a full crouch as the deceleration completed.
He held there for a moment, motionless, testing his body’s response.
Nothing had broken. Nothing had cracked. Nothing was even bruised.

He rose slowly to his full height, the compacted snow crunching softly under his boots as he shifted his weight. He rolled his shoulders. He flexed his hands. He tested each of his major joints in sequence.
Everything worked. He was, remarkably, completely uninjured.
He let out a long, slow breath into the frozen air.
"...That worked."

The exhale steamed white in the sub-zero air. Around him, the Antarctic interior stretched out in an endless white plain, the wind blowing hard across the flat, the sky above him a pale, elongated dusk of high-southern-latitude daylight, the horizon completely empty in every direction.
He was standing above the Spirit Pool. He was alive.
He was, by any honest reading, further ahead of every other party racing for the pool than he had any right to be.
He took a step forward.

Then he felt it. A cold, precise sensation at the back of his neck, not the cold of the wind, but a different kind of cold, the specific, primal cold that human survival instincts sent out when they detected something wrong in the environment. It was the sensation his body used to communicate predator.
He turned his head sharply. At the eastern horizon, four small streaks of movement were resolving out of the featureless white.
They were closing fast. Insanely fast.

He watched them for exactly one second. In that second, they crossed a distance that no human being, no vehicle, no aircraft, no living creature that he had ever seen documented, should have been able to cover on foot.

They were resolving into individual figures now, each one distinct, each one moving with the fluid, unstoppable rhythm of something that ran across the polar surface the way ordinary men walked across a room.
Two seconds. They were close enough now for him to see details.

Four figures. Male. Each of them shirtless in the sub-zero Antarctic air, their bare torsos steaming faintly with the raw, contained heat of bodies that were producing enough internal energy to make ambient temperature irrelevant. Each of them carrying his weight with the loose, ready quality of a physical athlete of a caliber Stan had never encountered before. Their faces were human. Their bearing was human. Their movement was not.
Three seconds. They arrived and surrounded him...

The four of them settled into a wide, encircling formation with the unhurried coordination of hunters closing on prey they were confident of, spacing themselves at four points of an equidistant circle roughly ten meters in radius, cutting off any possible exit vector. Their breathing was completely steady. None of them had broken a sweat, despite the fact that they had just crossed several kilometers of Antarctic surface in seconds.
The lead one, a lean, powerfully built man with dark eyes and long hair, looked Stan up and down with the quiet, assessing calm of a predator identifying the species of its meal.
He spoke. His voice was casual. Almost bored. "So livestocks are attracted to this spirit pool too."

Stan stood very still. The words landed in his ears with the specific weight of a term that had, in another era, been used to describe ordinary humans by beings who had considered themselves categorically superior. The book had used the same framing. Vampires, and, werewolves, regarded ordinary humans as little different from livestock.
The second man, taller, with a scar running from his jaw down into his collar, narrowed his eyes.
"There’s something strange in this one," he said. His voice was lower than the first man’s. "I can feel it. His aura is, unusual."
The third man tilted his head slightly. His hair was silver, though his face suggested he was no older than thirty.

"Don’t be afraid. He’s no True Human." The fourth man, the tallest of the four, and by the way the others’ attention deferred to him almost certainly the highest-ranked, simply watched Stan without speaking.

His eyes were pale, almost colorless, and there was a stillness in his gaze that made every other threat in the circle feel secondary. He was the one Stan should have been most afraid of. He knew it instantly.
Stan’s mind worked at high speed
’They said ’livestock.’ They said ’not a True Human.’ They know what a True Human is. They know the taxonomy of the old world. Then they should be of the old world.’

He picked his landing spot, a patch of relatively level snow, wind-packed and dense, roughly forty meters from the surface point above the Spirit Pool.
’Two seconds.’ He centered himself.
’One second!’
He hit the ice with full force!
The impact was enormous!
His feet drove into the compressed snow with the force of a heavy truck at highway speed.
His knees flexed, absorbing the initial shock, and his body continued downward into the powder as the momentum carried through his frame.
The snow beneath him crumpled and compacted around his boots.

The impact rippled outward through his skeleton in a wave of pressure that he felt, clearly, distinctly, the specific sensation of his bones registering the load and holding it, but did not break under.
His knees compressed to nearly a full crouch as the deceleration completed.
He held there for a moment, motionless, testing his body’s response.
Nothing had broken.
Nothing had cracked.
Nothing was even bruised.
He rose slowly to his full height, the compacted snow crunching softly under his boots as he shifted his weight.
He rolled his shoulders.
He flexed his hands.
He tested each of his major joints in sequence.
Everything worked.
He was, remarkably, completely uninjured.
He let out a long, slow breath into the frozen air.
"...That worked."
The exhale steamed white in the sub-zero air.

Around him, the Antarctic interior stretched out in an endless white plain, the wind blowing hard across the flat, the sky above him a pale, elongated dusk of high-southern-latitude daylight, the horizon completely empty in every direction.
He was standing above the Spirit Pool.
He was alive.
He was, by any honest reading, further ahead of every other party racing for the pool than he had any right to be.
He took a step forward.
Then he felt it.

A cold, precise sensation at the back of his neck, not the cold of the wind, but a different kind of cold, the specific, primal cold that human survival instincts sent out when they detected something wrong in the environment.
It was the sensation his body used to communicate predator.
He turned his head sharply.
At the eastern horizon, four small streaks of movement were resolving out of the featureless white.
They were closing fast.
Insanely fast.
He watched them for exactly one second.
In that second, they crossed a distance that no human being, no vehicle, no aircraft, no living creature that he had ever seen documented, should have been able to cover on foot.

They were resolving into individual figures now, each one distinct, each one moving with the fluid, unstoppable rhythm of something that ran across the polar surface the way ordinary men walked across a room.
Two seconds.
They were close enough now for him to see details.
Four figures.
Male.

Each of them shirtless in the sub-zero Antarctic air, their bare torsos steaming faintly with the raw, contained heat of bodies that were producing enough internal energy to make ambient temperature irrelevant.
Each of them carrying his weight with the loose, ready quality of a physical athlete of a caliber Stan had never encountered before.
Their faces were human.
Their bearing was human.
Their movement was not.
Three seconds.
They arrived and surrounded him...

The four of them settled into a wide, encircling formation with the unhurried coordination of hunters closing on prey they were confident of, spacing themselves at four points of an equidistant circle roughly ten meters in radius, cutting off any possible exit vector.
Their breathing was completely steady.
None of them had broken a sweat, despite the fact that they had just crossed several kilometers of Antarctic surface in seconds.
The lead one, a lean, powerfully built man with dark eyes and long hair, looked Stan up and down with the quiet, assessing calm of a predator identifying the species of its meal.
He spoke.
His voice was casual.
Almost bored.
"So livestocks are attracted to this spirit pool too."
Stan stood very still.
The words landed in his ears with the specific weight of a term that had, in another era, been used to describe ordinary humans by beings who had considered themselves categorically superior.
The book had used the same framing.
Vampires, and, werewolves, regarded ordinary humans as little different from livestock.
The second man, taller, with a scar running from his jaw down into his collar, narrowed his eyes.
"There’s something strange in this one," he said.
His voice was lower than the first man’s.
"I can feel it.
His aura is, unusual."
The third man tilted his head slightly.
His hair was silver, though his face suggested he was no older than thirty.
"Don’t be afraid.
He’s no True Human." The fourth man, the tallest of the four, and by the way the others’ attention deferred to him almost certainly the highest-ranked, simply watched Stan without speaking.
His eyes were pale, almost colorless, and there was a stillness in his gaze that made every other threat in the circle feel secondary.
He was the one Stan should have been most afraid of.
He knew it instantly.
Stan’s mind worked at high speed
’They said ’livestock.’ They said ’not a True Human.’ They know what a True Human is.
They know the taxonomy of the old world.
Then they should be of the old world.’

chapters.title: Chapter 314: Surrounded by Predators
paragraphs: Stan’s mind worked at high speed. ’They said ’livestock.’ They said ’not a True Human.’ They know what a True Human is. They know the taxonomy of the old world. Then they should be of the old world.’ He looked around the circle.
The bodies. The speed. The bare chests in sub-zero air. The casual predator’s confidence.
’What are they? Vampires? Werewolves? Or demihumans? Or something from the same era? They didn’t vanish. Or at least, not all of them did. They’ve come back.’
’They can’t be Werewolves or demi humans, if not there should obvious features on their bodies... That leaves the last option, are they Vampires?’
He was just speculating, he can’t say for sure if his guesses were right or wrong... He kept his face composed.

’They were attracted here by my plane. Or by the noise. Or by both. If I hadn’t stored the aircraft when I did, they would have destroyed it themselves before I ever reached the pool. And me with it. I don’t know why I feel this way, but why do I feel like they can handle the plane’s explosion with relative ease.’
’They are here to guard the Spirit Pool. Or to claim it. Or both.’
’They are, individually, almost certainly stronger than I am.’
He assessed himself against them with cold, honest precision.

His current strength baseline was extraordinary by ordinary human standards. He could lift objects that no ordinary human could lift. He could take impacts that would kill an ordinary human. He was, by every measure of the modern era, an outlier.
But he was not, he realized instantly, at their level.
They were operating in a different physiological register entirely. Their speed alone had been beyond anything he could match.

Their bodies were putting out more raw kinetic capability than his own by a margin he could visibly see. His current strength probably placed him at somewhere between a quarter and a half of any one of theirs. And there were four of them.
The odds were not good. The odds were, in fact, terrible.

The four of them held their positions in the circle for a long, silent second. Stan stood in the center, his backpack still on his shoulders, his coat still zipped against the polar wind, his hands loose and empty at his sides.
The standoff lasted exactly one second longer. Then the lead man moved. And the other three moved with him.

They came at Stan from four directions simultaneously, at speeds that no ordinary eye could have tracked, closing the ten-meter gap with the fluid, coordinated economy of predators executing a killing formation they had performed a thousand times before.
Stan’s body, wired for combat by the martial arts mastery he had installed less than a day earlier, responded instantly.
He moved. The four of them moved as well...
They moved the way weather moved. The way tidal waves moved. The way things moved when the laws of nature had temporarily agreed to look the other way.
Stan’s body responded before his mind did.

The martial mastery installed in his consciousness took over the moment the first strike came. His feet shifted. His weight dropped. His right arm rose in a hard, angled block that intercepted a fist the size of his own head at a speed he could not have tracked without his current dilated perception after tempering...
The impact cracked through his forearm like a truck slamming into a wall.

He was already turning. His left leg swept back, his hip rotating, his body threading between the two other strikes that were closing on him from behind. He caught the third fist on the back of his elbow. He redirected the fourth strike into empty air with the smallest, most efficient parry his mastery could produce.
Four attacks in the span of one heartbeat.
He had survived them. Barely.
Not daring to waste time, He counterattacked.

His right fist rocketed toward the lead man’s chin. Straight, focused, backed by the full weight of his tempered skeleton and every ounce of enhanced strength his body could produce. It was a strike that would have shattered concrete. It was a strike that would have killed an ordinary human instantly.
The lead man tilted his head three centimeters to the left.
Stan’s fist tore through empty air. The lead man smiled. Then he moved.
The next fifteen seconds happened at a speed that Stan’s mind could not fully process.
They were everywhere.

The four of them attacked from four angles simultaneously, their bodies phasing in and out of his peripheral vision as blurs of motion, dark hair, bare torsos, the flash of eyes catching the polar light.
Every strike was aimed at a vital point. The temples. The throat. The heart. The base of the spine. His liver. His kidney. His diaphragm.
His body defended itself.
His forearms rose. His elbows tucked. His knees lifted to intercept the low kicks aimed at his hamstrings.

His head turned by microscopic increments to slip strikes that would have crushed his skull. His mastery was reading every attack a fraction of a second before it arrived, and his tempered body was executing the defensive movements with the effortless precision of a discipline he should have spent decades acquiring.
He blocked one strike. He blocked another. He blocked seven more.
He caught the eighth on his shoulder and it drove him backward two meters through the compacted snow.
He blocked the ninth. He blocked the tenth. He blocked the eleventh. The twelfth caught him on the ribs.
Something inside his chest made a small, terrible sound.
He staggered. But he kept blocking. He couldn’t afford to slack, any mistake meant death...
Fists met forearms in a rolling, thundering cascade that produced its own weather system around them. The ice at their feet fractured outward in spider-web patterns.

The wind was displaced by the shockwaves of their exchanges, small vortices of polar air spinning off in tight, angry spirals. The steam of the bare-chested men’s body heat swirled around Stan as he moved between them.
They were smiling. All four of them.

They wore the small, delighted expressions of predators who had been given something interesting to play with, the specific, insulting smile of hunters who had discovered that their prey had teeth, and were amusing themselves by finding out how long the teeth could last.

chapters.title: Chapter 315: One Percent
paragraphs: Stan’s mastery was operating at full capacity. But they were still faster than he could match.

The realization landed in the back of his mind with cold, precise clarity. He was blocking their attacks. He was intercepting their strikes. He was doing better than any modern human had any right to do against beings of this caliber. But they were playing with him.
They had not, in any meaningful sense, actually been trying to hurt him.
The specific, stinging humiliation of the moment cut through his focus.

He gritted his teeth and pushed harder, his body accelerating fractionally, his strikes carrying more weight, his blocks becoming more aggressive counters. The mastery in his mind supplied every technique it had. He was, by any honest measure, fighting at the peak of what his current physiology could produce.
The four men laughed hysterically...
’They’re laughing...’ Stan gritted his teeth...

The lead one, the one Stan had already identified as the most dangerous, caught Stan’s next strike with an open palm, closed his fingers around Stan’s fist, and simply held him there. Motionless. As if Stan’s arm had been made of paper.
Then he shoved. Stan was sent flying...
He tore backward through the polar air for twelve meters before his body hit the snow again, plowing through it in a long, spreading trench of white and ice.
He rolled to his feet.

The system’s map arrow was still fixed in his vision, glowing at the edge of his awareness. The Spirit Pool was somewhere in the direction he had been thrown from. He had, for the past minute or so, been moving progressively further away from it.
The four men, stood in a loose formation across the snow, watching him with unhurried, delighted patience.
The realization arrived in Stan’s mind with a kind of terrible completeness.
He was not going to reach the Spirit Pool. Not through these four. Not with his current strength. Not remotely. It was simply impossible.
He understood, in that moment, what the old world had actually been like. What the ’Introduction to Earth’ had been describing when it had used the word ’livestock’ on normal humans.

This was what humanity had lived with, for thousands of years, before the Night of Vanishing. This casual, effortless superiority. This complete and unquestioned confidence that ordinary humans were simply ’lesser’, beneath consideration, below the register at which real beings operated.
The old world was returning. And it was returning brutal.
The leadee raised a hand.
The other three stopped.

They straightened out of their attacking stances with the unified, coordinated calm of predators responding to a single leader. The polar wind picked up around them, sending long strands of their dark hair drifting sideways in the breeze. The steam rising off their bare torsos hazed the air between Stan and the four of them.
The lead one looked at Stan. The smile was still there.
"Kid." His voice was casual. "Are you from the Realm’s portal too, or are you a New Age human of this world?"

Stan said nothing. He did not have breath to spare on answers. His ribs on his left side had been fractured. His forearms were bruised down to the bone. His body was operating on adrenaline and system-tempered endurance, and he could feel, distantly, that both were finite.
The leader’s expression did not change. But when Stan didn’t answer, Stan immediately sensed that something had changed, these beings whatever they were, was annoyed now...
The leader’s face remain chill and calm as he began;

"You see," he said quietly, "I don’t think you understand your position. When I ask you a question, you’re supposed to answer. Because, in case you couldn’t tell, we’ve been playing with you throughout this entire encounter. We haven’t used one percent of our strength."
He stepped forward casually, and then with a slight smile, he flexed his right hand as he walked.
Stan watched as the skin of the werewolf’s hand rippled and thick, coarse dark-gray fur erupted from every follicle in a slow, deliberate wave that traveled from his wrist to the tips of his fingers.
His fingernails elongated, thickened, curved into hooked black claws that looked more like the talons of a predator than anything belonging to a humanoid.

The bone structure beneath the fur shifted, the knuckles enlarging, the tendons becoming visible through the fur, the entire hand transforming from something human into something distinctly, unmistakably lupine.
Stan’s mind raced. ’The fur pattern. The bone structure. The rate of transformation.’
’Are they werewolves, I thought they were gone. The book was right. Or is that they didn’t vanish permanently. They came back. Or they never left. Or...’

’They can change parts of their bodies at will. They’re not locked in either form. They’re both, at will. And they can control the ratio. I can’t believe Ive been fighting werewolves this entire time and didn’t know it.’
He remembered reading, as a teenager, novels about werewolves who transformed fully under the full moon. That had never been what these beings actually were. The reality was more terrifying.

They could weaponize any part of themselves, at any moment, without committing to a full transformation. They were not humans who occasionally became wolves. They were something older than either. Real Werewolves were thousands of times stronger than those beings depicted in movies...
Meanwhile, the werewolf casually lifted his transformed hand and looked at it appreciatively.
The air around him seemed to compress.
Stan’s mastery-trained senses registered the change immediately. The aura around the werewolf had multiplied. It had jumped, visibly, palpably, in a single instant, by a factor of at least five.
The version of this being that Stan had struggled to match a moment ago was gone.
This version could kill him without effort. That former version could probably still kill Stan too of they were not playing with him...
A cold bead of sweat traced down Stan’s temple.
’Fuck.’
The thought was the only articulate response his mind could produce.
’I’m actually going to die.’
He assessed his options with cold, mechanical precision. He had to be honest with himself as he no longer had the luxury of hoping.

Flight was impossible. The werewolves’ base speed had already exceeded his top speed by several times over. With even one of them partially transformed, the gap would be impossible to close. He would be caught within seconds of turning away.

chapters.title: Chapter 316: The Plaything
paragraphs: There was no option. Fighting was impossible. He had already been outmatched at their playing pace. Their real pace would end him in a single exchange.
Negotiation was impossible. They had already told him what he was; livestock. The word implied everything he needed to know about how negotiation would be received.

The system was silent. He mentally reached out to it, this was the greatest danger he had faced since its activation, but he found nothing, no solution he could think of. No notifications. No emergency prompts. No hidden protocols the mission designer might have inserted for exactly this scenario.
He was alone. He could only watch as the werewolf’s smile widened.
"You see," he said gently, "this is barely two percent of my strength, and you’re already sweating this hard."
Saying that, the werewolf kept walking casually.
Then all of a sudden, he vanished!
One heartbeat, the werewolf was ten meters away. The next, he was standing beside Stan, instantly blitzing Stan with insane speed.
He raised one clawed hand and flicked his finger.
The flick, casual, dismissive, the kind of gesture a bored man might use to swat away an insect, created a small compression wave in the polar air.
Stan felt the wave pass through him a fraction of a second before the flick itself connected with his midsection.
The impact hit him like a truck at highway speed.
His body launched. He tore backward through the air at speeds his own recent flight training told him were somewhere near the low subsonic range.

He hit the ice fifty meters later and tunneled through it, plowing a trench through the compacted snow and ice for another thirty meters before his momentum bled out and his body came to a shuddering stop.
The pain arrived a full second after the impact.
He looked down. There was a hole in his stomach.

A gaping, ragged, ugly hole where the werewolf’s fingernail had connected, his abdominal wall opened cleanly, the layers of tissue beneath visible in the wound, a section of his intestines exposed to the polar air. The werewolf had opened him up with a single finger flick, at two percent of his true capacity, as casually as a man tearing paper.
Stan tried to breathe. The breath came out through the hole in his stomach as well as through his mouth.

Something in his mind detached from the immediate reality of the injury, the way trauma made minds detach when their owners had no capacity left to process what was happening to their bodies. He looked at the wound. He noted, dispassionately, that he could see his own organs. He was in so much pain...
Meanwhile, the werewolf appeared beside him. He crouched down.
He placed one clawed hand on the back of Stan’s head, the fur soft against Stan’s scalp, the claws cool against his temples, and pressed Stan’s face down into the ice.
Then he began to ’drag’ him.
He flew forward casually across the snow, his hand pinning Stan’s head in place, dragging Stan’s face along the ice at whatever pace he chose to walk at.

Stan’s cheek and forehead abraded against the compacted snow. His skin tore. His flesh scraped down layer by layer. A long, spreading trail of red painted the white ice behind them as the werewolf strolled leisurely across the polar surface.
The werewolf spoke as he walked.

"You see, if you were from the Realm’s portal, you should’ve then be a Cultivator in at least Genesis Realm. But I can’t sense your Qi, which should be impossible for anyone at that level. So you’re not from the portal."
He continued dragging.
"But I can smell Divine Bronze on you."
Stan’s face left red on the ice.

"Now that’s interesting. If you’re not from the portal, then how did a New Age creature like you get his hands on Divine Bronze? That’s an old-world treasure. That’s a high-tier old-world treasure. Livestock like you shouldn’t be within a hundred kilometers of anything like that."

He grabbed Stan by the ankle and hurled him.

Stan flew roughly... He hit a distant ice ridge and shattered through it, his body carving a chunk of the frozen ridge out with the sheer force of his passage before landing in a heap on the far side.

Every bone in his body, even the ones that his tempered skeleton had made five times stronger, was screaming with the accumulated damage of injuries that would have killed a normal human twenty times over.
The werewolf appeared above him again. He crouched. He picked Stan up by the throat.
He held him at arm’s length, the polar wind whipping around them, Stan’s blood dripping down onto the ice below in a slow, steady patter.

"You’re not much of a toy," he said conversationally. "You break too easily. New Age humans are so fragile. No wonder your entire species let itself be reduced to what it is now, but I don’t get why you’re more resilient than the others."

He casually drew one claw across Stan’s chest. Skin parted. Muscle parted. The claw ran from his collarbone to his hip in a single, effortless cut. Stan’s body opened along the line like a canvas being scored by a knife.
Stan tried to scream again. His throat produced only a wet, ragged sound.

chapters.title: Chapter 317: One Last Theory
paragraphs: Stan tried to scream again but his throat produced only a wet, ragged sound.

The werewolf smiled and tossed him aside. Stan hit the ice again. He did not have the strength to roll. He lay on his back in the snow, his blood pooling around him in a spreading circle, and stared up at the pale Antarctic sky.
The werewolf stood over him.

The other three watched from a distance, statue-still, their expressions carrying the small, contemptuous amusement of hunters who had confirmed that the prey was not worth their personal effort and were content to let their leader take his time.
The werewolf’s smile had not changed. It had not changed at all.

For the entire duration of the mutilation, the throwing, the dragging, the scoring, the crushing, his face had held exactly the same calm, faintly interested, faintly amused expression. As if none of what he was doing was of any consequence to him. As if breaking Stan into pieces was simply an aesthetic exercise.
’It’s nothing to him,’ Stan realized distantly. ’Nothing. This is nothing.’
He lay in the snow.

His body was not functional in any meaningful sense. His abdomen was open. His chest was open. His face was ground down to the bone in patches. Blood was leaving him in volumes that his physiology, even in its enhanced state, could not sustain. He was breathing in short, wet, gurgling gasps.
He should have been dead.
He was, distantly, aware that the only reason he was not dead was that the werewolf was letting him remain alive. The wounds should have killed him.

The blood loss should have killed him. The werewolves’ pride, apparently, had been offended enough by his attempt to fight back that the lead one had specifically decided to prolong the killing to teach him a lesson. But that didn’t change the fact that he’s at his last breath...
’Am I going to die like this?’ His mind was drifting.

He thought of the ’Introduction to Earth’. The book had said the vampires and werewolves had vanished during the Night of Vanishing. But the book had also said something else, that no one knew where they had gone. That they might one day return.
The werewolf standing over him had spoken of a Realm’s portal.
Stan’s fragmenting mind, working on whatever cognitive fuel remained, made the connection.

The system’s scan had detected a portal. A divine portal. The book had implied that the vanished races had gone somewhere. What if they had gone to a realm, a separate space, connected to Earth by portals, where the ambient Qi still existed at the levels the old world had known?
What if the recent appearance of the Spirit Pool was not just the return of Qi to Earth’s surface, but the bleeding through of that other realm into the world Stan had grown up in?
It didn’t make sense but this was just Stan’s guess.
The werewolves were not returning humans. They were coming through.
He filed the theory away with the small, dim clarity of a mind that was running out of time to think about anything.
No matter what he had to survive somehow... He shouldn’t die here in the middle of nowhere with his girls waiting for him...

The lead werewolf kicked him again. This time, the kick landed directly in the open wound of his abdomen. Stan felt his insides shift. He coughed a great mouthful of blood into the snow beside his head.
The werewolf laughed appreciatively.

"You’re still conscious. That’s actually impressive. New Age humans usually stop responding around this stage. What are you made of, kid? That Divine bronze pill you took is pretty good stuff even for trash like you..."
Stan did not answer. He could not answer. His mind was doing the last calculation it was capable of.
’The inventory.’
The thought arrived like a distant, quiet whisper.

He had used it earlier that morning without qi expenditure. He had willed objects into it and out of it. It operated at the speed of intention. The system had said, when he purchased it, that it required no qi consumption.
He tried it.
His mind reached out toward the werewolf standing over him. The werewolf’s body was, functionally, an object. The inventory was, functionally, a spatial pocket that could store objects.
Stan willed.
The system responded instantly.
[The object possesses will and resists spatial storage.]
Stan cursed silently. ’Fuck... Damn it! Of course.’
The inventory could not simply eat a sentient being. The werewolf had a will. His will was actively resisting the storage attempt. It was, in retrospect, obvious.

If the inventory could just consume any being that Stan chose to target, then he would have been able to eliminate every threat he had ever faced with a single mental effort. That was not how the world worked.
The werewolf’s smile widened suddenly. "...Now what was that?"
His nostrils flared. His eyes narrowed. He tilted his head at Stan with an expression that had shifted from casual amusement into something sharper and more attentive.
"What was that little spatial technique? That was interesting."

He crouched down again. He grabbed Stan by the collar and hauled him up until Stan’s face was inches from his own. His breath, when he spoke, smelled faintly of bronze and something wilder, the specific animal warmth of a predator.

"You just tried to store me, didn’t you." His voice was very quiet now. Very intent. "Live-stock actually dares to attempt a spatial technique on me. You’re quite stubborn, I just thought you a lesson but you just won’t learn."
He looked genuinely offended.

He blitzed sideways in a blur that Stan’s enhanced perception could not track and reappeared behind Stan, one claw pressed lightly against the base of Stan’s neck. The tip of the claw was cold against Stan’s spine. Stan could feel it touching his neck bones, the werewolf had cut through enough of Stan’s neck tissue to actually be resting his claw against the bone itself.

"I could take your head right now," the werewolf said conversationally. "But I want to know what you did. What was that? I didn’t even sense any Qi fluctuations. Where did you get a spatial storage technique of that quality? Answer me, and I’ll make the ending quick."
Stan did not answer. His mind was working on one last theory.

chapters.title: Chapter 318: A Gamble Against Death!
paragraphs: "But I want to know what you did. What was that? I didn’t even sense any Qi fluctuations. Where did you get a spatial storage technique of that quality? Answer me, and I’ll make the ending quick."
Stan did not answer. His mind was working on one last theory.
He could not store the werewolf. The werewolf had will.
But while he himself had will, he won’t resist the inventory.
The inventory followed his will, so his will is the will of the inventory, so if this worked then he would, in theory, exist inside the inventory space until he willed himself back out.
It was a theory. It was a terrible theory.

He had no idea whether the inventory could contain a living being at all. He had no idea whether his consciousness would survive the storage attempt. He had no idea whether he would be able to will himself back out. He might dissolve. He might cease to exist. He might spend the rest of eternity inside a spatial pocket with no way to reach anything outside it.
The alternative was having his head removed by a werewolf claw in the next several seconds.
He decided. He took the last shallow, ragged breath his lungs could produce.
He focused then willed the inventory to consume him.
The werewolf’s clawed hand tightened on the back of Stan’s neck. The claw began to press.
Stan felt the first fraction of a second of the pressure that was about to sever his spine.
And then he vanished. Not sideways. Not upward. Not in any direction that the werewolf could see.
He was simply, in that instant, not present in the polar air anymore.
The werewolf’s hand closed on empty space. His claw sliced through nothing. His eyes went wide.
He straightened up abruptly, spinning on his heels, scanning the ice around him with the sudden, sharp alertness of a predator who had just watched his prey execute a technique he did not recognize.
The other three werewolves converged on his position in an instant.
The four of them stood in a tight formation, scanning the empty polar landscape.
There was no sign of Stan.

There was no scent trail. No footprints. No blood spatter leading in any direction. The pool of blood that had been beneath him was still there, staining the snow crimson, but the body that had been producing it was simply gone.
The lead werewolf’s face darkened.
"...Where did he go."

None of the others answered. They stood in the polar wind, staring at the empty space where Stan Harrison had been a heartbeat before, the mystery of his disappearance sitting between them like a puzzle none of them had any framework to solve.
Stan opened his eyes. He was floating.

He was, more accurately, existing, in a space that was neither dark nor light, neither warm nor cold, that had no visible boundaries and no discernible dimensions. It did not feel like a room. It did not feel like a container. It felt like an absence, the specific absence of a place that was not intended for living things to occupy.
But he was alive. And, for the moment, he was somewhere no werewolf could reach him.
He let out a long, slow, uneven breath.
’It worked!’

The theory had held. He was inside his own inventory space, contained by the same infrastructure that had stored the Bone-Tempering Pill’s empty container, the Jade Purity Elixir’s bottle, the ’Introduction to Earth’ book, the Dao Language primer, and, as of a few hours earlier, an entire long-range polar aircraft.
He tried to move his arm. It did not move.
He tried again, still nothing.

His arm did not respond. Neither did his legs. Neither did his fingers. His entire body was locked in place, suspended in the neutral non-space of the inventory as though something had frozen him at the cellular level.
He tried to speak. His lips did not move. He tried to draw a fresh breath. His lungs did not respond. The realization arrived cleanly.
’Time. Space is locked, and time with it. The inventory freezes everything inside it, that’s how items don’t decay. That’s how the pill and elixir stayed potent.’
’But as the owner, I’m partially exempt. My mind is still running. My body isn’t. The space affects me the way it affects everything else, but the time freeze, my consciousness is outside it.’
He assessed rapidly.

His body was locked in its exact injured state. His wounds were still there, the hole in his abdomen, the torn chest, the ground-down face, but they were also frozen. The blood that had been pouring out of him had stopped at the exact moment he had entered the inventory. He was not, in this moment, actively dying. The catastrophic blood loss that had been about to kill him seconds ago had been paused mid-process.
But so had his breathing.

His last breath, the shallow, ragged one he had taken before triggering the inventory, was the only breath he had. He could not draw another one. His body’s oxygen reserves would carry him for a limited window, and after that, he would suffocate.
He estimated it.

In his current state, with severe injuries, blood loss, and the accumulated damage of the fight, he could probably hold what remained in his lungs for around thirty seconds before his brain began to fail. In his prime, he might have managed forty to fifty. In this state, thirty was optimistic.
Thirty seconds. That was his window.
He had thirty seconds to wait out the werewolves outside, and then he had to leave the inventory before he suffocated.
He forced his mind to remain calm. He counted.
’One.’
’Two.’
’Three.’
Outside the inventory, on the Antarctic ice, the lead werewolf stood over the empty patch of red-soaked snow where Stan had been a moment earlier.
His face carried an expression it had not carried once during the entire encounter, genuine, focused disbelief.

"He’s gone." He crouched. He ran a clawed finger through the pool of blood on the ice. The blood was fresh. The scent was fresh. Every physical trace suggested Stan had been in this exact location a heartbeat ago. And yet the body itself had simply ceased to be present in the polar air.
"He actually escaped." He tilted his head, sniffing the air. There was no trail. There was no scent moving in any direction. There was no residual heat signature disappearing into the distance.
There was no evidence at all that Stan Harrison had moved from this spot. He had, from every physical measurement the werewolf could perform, simply stopped existing.
"What kind of life-saving treasure was that." His voice was low. The casual amusement of the previous minutes was completely gone.
The werewolf’s eyes were sharp now, calculating, the expression of a predator who had discovered that his prey had possessed a defensive tool he had not been able to categorize.
"This human is not simple."
